---
name: grill-me
description: A relentless interview to sharpen a plan or design.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Call the Skill tool with "grilling".
---
name: grilling
description: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
---

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs live in [LibreLift/libre-lift](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues).
Use the `gh` CLI with `--repo LibreLift/libre-lift` for issue operations. The local
origin still uses the former `LibreLift/expo_suite` name, which GitHub redirects.

Read [project management](../project-mgmt.md) before tracker changes. Use its
issue templates, milestone rules, assignment process, and definition of done.

## Issue operations

- Read: `gh issue view NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --comments`.
- List: `gh issue list --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --state open --json number,title,labels,assignees`.
- Create: `gh issue create --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --title TITLE --body-file FILE --label LABEL`.
- Comment: `gh issue comment NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --body-file FILE`.
- Labels: `gh issue edit NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --add-label LABEL --remove-label LABEL`.
- Close: `gh issue close NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --reason REASON`;
  use `completed` for delivered work or `not planned` for declined/superseded work.

Write multiline bodies to a file and pass `--body-file`. Use the matching
`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` structure. During triage, every published issue or comment
must start with `> *This was generated by AI during triage.*`.

## Project board

The board is [LibreLift MVP, organization project 1](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1).
Issue labels and board fields are separate. Use the mapping in
[triage labels](./triage-labels.md) for readiness and execution roles.

Inspect current fields with `gh project field-list 1 --owner LibreLift --format json`
and items with `gh project item-list 1 --owner LibreLift --format json`. Resolve
current project, field, item, and option IDs before a board edit; use
`gh project item-edit` for field changes. Check view filters before treating an
item as absent. Reuse the existing Status and Task Size fields and their options.

Project reads require the `read:project` token scope; writes require `project`.
If CLI access is unavailable, the public board can be inspected read-only. Report
blocked board edits and leave them pending rather than claiming synchronization.

## Dependencies and claiming work

Use native GitHub sub-issues for epics and native issue dependencies for blockers.
If unavailable, record `Part of #NUMBER` and `Blocked by: #NUMBER` links in the
issue body. A blocked task is not Ready. Apply `planned work` only with maintainer
authorization; follow the repository's assignment process before claiming work.

When a skill says to publish a spec or fetch a ticket, create or read a GitHub
issue in this repository. Follow repository label mappings instead of creating
labels named after a skill or its internal roles.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.**
# Domain documentation

LibreLift has one domain context, with a root glossary and shared ADR directory.

Before exploring domain code, designing a change, or naming concepts in issues,
tests, and documentation:

1. Read [GLOSSARY.md](../../GLOSSARY.md) and use its canonical terms.
2. Read the relevant records in [docs/adr/](../adr/README.md).
3. For the initial UI, read the [foundation decisions](../ui-foundation.md).

Keep the glossary limited to domain meanings. Record implementation choices in
the design documentation or an ADR when the decision has a consequential trade-off.
Surface contradictions with an existing term or ADR before changing its meaning.
Use the domain-modeling flow to resolve gaps and update documentation as decisions
are agreed. If a referenced domain document is absent, continue; create it when
there is a resolved term or decision to record.

# Project Management

The [LibreLift MVP project board](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1)
tracks planned work, priorities, and progress. Use the Plan view to see task sizes
and milestone groupings, and the Backlog view to follow workflow states. Check
the view's filters if an expected issue is not visible.

## Requests and triage

Use the repository's issue templates to report a problem, suggest a feature, or
request a documentation change. Feature and bug templates apply `needs triage`;
a request is not a commitment to implement it.

Maintainers review requests for scope, clarity, duplicates, and dependencies.
They ask for missing context, explain decisions on the issue, and either close
the request with a reason, defer it, or turn accepted work into actionable tasks.
Only maintainers apply `planned work`, so contributors can distinguish agreed
work from requests still under discussion. When a broad request is replaced by
smaller tasks, link the replacements and explain that closing the request does
not mean its implementation is complete.

## Planned work, epics, and milestones

Use the Task template for agreed work. Each task should describe its goal,
context and related design links, checkable acceptance criteria, dependencies,
and where to start. Size tasks with the board's Task Size field: XS is up to
one hour, S is two hours, M is four hours, L is seven hours, and XL is more than
seven hours. Split work that contains independently useful, reviewable changes.

Group feature tasks under a parent issue labeled `epic`, using GitHub
sub-issues. Epics describe user-visible outcomes; shared setup tasks can remain
standalone when several epics depend on them. Link dependencies so contributors
can see what must be finished first.

Assign planned work to the milestone it supports:

- **M1: Runnable Demo — November 18, 2026:** account access, exercise selection,
  and creating, saving, reopening, editing, and deleting fixed-weight templates.
- **M2: MVP — December 2, 2026:** workout logging and history, personal exercise
  maximums, percentage-based targets, and deferred catalog caching/retry work.

The M1 milestone description records capacity, estimates, and scope cuts.
Maintainers keep milestone assignments and board priorities aligned with that
budget. See the [roadmap](./roadmap.md) for work beyond the MVP.

## Workflow states

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Backlog | Work is recorded but is not ready to start. |
| Ready | Scope and acceptance criteria are clear and prerequisites are available. |
| In progress | An assigned contributor is actively working on the issue. |
| In review | The implementation PR is ready for independent review. |
| Done | The change has met the [definition of done](./git-standards.md#definition-of-done). |

Keep issue and board status current as work moves. A blocked task should not be
treated as ready until its prerequisites are resolved. Closed requests that were
superseded or declined should be distinguished from completed implementation in
their closing explanation.

## Labels and choosing work

| Label | How to use it |
| --- | --- |
| `needs triage` | A request awaits a maintainer's decision. |
| `planned work` | Maintainer-approved work available for planning and assignment. |
| `epic` | A parent issue grouping work by the value it delivers. |
| `good first issue` | A task intended to help newcomers get started; check dependencies and Ready status before choosing it. |
| `enhancement` | A feature suggestion or improvement; check triage status before implementing it. |
| `documentation` | A documentation addition or correction. |
| `help wanted` | Community assistance is requested. |
| `question` | Further information is requested from the issue author. |
| `awaiting response` | The issue author is waiting for communication from a maintainer. |

Start with an unassigned Ready task, preferably a `good first issue` for your
first contribution. Read its acceptance criteria and dependencies, then request
assignment through GitHub Discussions as described in the
[communication standards](./communication-standards.md). Ask about blocked
work before starting it to avoid duplicating effort.
# LibreLift

LibreLift helps individuals plan reusable workouts, record their performance,
and review their workout history. These terms distinguish planned training from
what happened during a particular session.

## Language

### People and access

**User**:
A person who plans and records their training in LibreLift and owns their workout
templates and workout sessions.

**Account**:
The identity through which a user signs in and accesses their saved training data.
_Avoid_: User when referring specifically to sign-in identity

**Account name**:
The name a user chooses to display for their account. It can be changed without
changing the email address used to sign in.
_Avoid_: Username when implying a unique sign-in identifier

### Planning

**Exercise**:
A movement, such as a bench press or squat, described by its name, target muscles,
and equipment.

**Exercise catalog**:
The collection of exercises available for inclusion in workout templates.
_Avoid_: Workout catalog, template library

**Catalog exercise**:
A named movement in the exercise catalog, with an identity shared by every template
or session that references it.
_Avoid_: Template exercise, session exercise

**Primary muscles**:
The muscles identified by the catalog as the main targets of an exercise. Missing
targets remain unspecified rather than being inferred.
_Avoid_: All target muscles

**Secondary muscles**:
The muscles identified by the catalog as supporting targets of an exercise,
distinct from its primary muscles. Missing targets remain unspecified rather than
being inferred.
_Avoid_: Primary muscles

**Muscle group**:
A broader category of muscles described by a familiar training label, such as
Chest, Upper back, Lower back, or Calves.
_Avoid_: Primary muscle when referring to the broader category

**No equipment**:
An exercise's explicit lack of required equipment, identified from the catalog's
bodyweight designation when equipment is absent. Missing equipment without that
designation is not evidence that no equipment is required.
_Avoid_: Unknown equipment

**Workout template**:
A reusable workout description containing exercises and their planned sets.
“Template” is its short name.
_Avoid_: Plan, routine (as separate domain concepts)

**Template draft**:
Unsaved changes to a workout template. These changes are separate from the saved
template until the user saves them.

**Template exercise**:
A placement of a catalog exercise within a workout template, with its own identity,
saved exercise details, and planned sets. The same catalog exercise can appear in
multiple placements; catalog changes do not change saved templates.
_Avoid_: Exercise when referring specifically to its inclusion in a template

**Template set**:
A planned set for a template exercise, with a target weight and target repetition
count.
_Avoid_: Round

### Performing and reviewing

**Workout session**:
One occurrence of performing a workout based on a workout template. “Session” is
its short name.
_Avoid_: Workout when the distinction from a workout template matters

**Session exercise**:
A placement of a catalog exercise within a workout session, with its own identity,
saved exercise details, and session sets. Its catalog identity is retained, and
catalog changes do not change saved workout history.
_Avoid_: Template exercise when referring to a session's exercise

**Session set**:
A set belonging to a session exercise, with planned targets and the performance
recorded for that session.
_Avoid_: Round, template set when referring to a session's set

**Workout history**:
The collection of saved past workout sessions available for review.
_Avoid_: Workout log, log (as names for a separate domain concept)

### Sets and performance

**Repetition**:
One performance of an exercise's movement. “Rep” is its short name.

**Set**:
A group of repetitions of one exercise; it belongs to that exercise rather than
grouping several exercises together.
_Avoid_: Round, circuit

**Target performance**:
The planned weight and repetition count for a set.
_Avoid_: Goal when referring specifically to a set's targets

**Fixed-weight target**:
A target weight expressed directly as an amount of weight.

**Personal exercise maximum**:
The weight a user records as their maximum for one repetition of a particular
exercise. It is the reference weight for percentage-based targets.

**Percentage-based target**:
A target weight expressed as a percentage of the user's personal maximum for that
exercise.

**Recorded performance**:
The weight and repetition count recorded for a session set, which may differ from
its target performance. “Actual” is a synonym for these recorded values.

# LibreLift roadmap

LibreLift provides free workout planning and logging for individual users. This
roadmap follows the project proposal's feature priorities: P0 is the minimum viable
product (MVP), P1 is the next step, and P2 is longer-term exploration. Work after
the MVP has no committed release dates.

## MVP

The semester MVP lets a user create and reuse workout templates using exercises
from a catalog, start workout sessions using existing templates, and review saved
workout history. It also supports recording exercise maximums and calculating
target weights as percentages of those maximums. These functions are available
without a subscription or payment.

The MVP is scoped to two delivery milestones:

| Milestone | Target date | What a user can do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [M1: Runnable Demo](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/milestone/1) | November 18, 2026 | Sign in, choose catalog exercises, and create, save, reopen, edit, and delete a workout template with fixed target weights and repetitions. Workout logging and maximum-based calculations are deferred to M2. |
| [M2: MVP](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/milestone/2) | December 2, 2026 | Start a workout from a saved template, record actual weights and repetitions, complete or stop the workout, and review its saved history. Record personal exercise maximums and use percentages to calculate template target weights. |

Templates and workout history must persist across app restarts. Editing or reusing
a template must not alter previously logged workouts. The first milestone covers
the complete template-creation workflow; the second adds the workout-logging
workflow and percentage-based planning.

The features below are deferred from the MVP to keep the semester build focused
on these core workflows within the available development time. Contributors can
help with implementation, testing, and documentation; see the
[contribution guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) and
[project board](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1) for how to get involved
and what work is currently planned.

## Next

These P1 features extend the MVP once the core planning and logging workflows
are established. Their order below follows the CP3 proposal.

1. **Integrated rest timer.** Add a rest timer to the workout experience. This is
   next because it improves an existing workflow without introducing a separate
   product area. It is deferred from the MVP because a timer is not required to
   record a workout. Contributors can help design the controls, implement the
   timer, and test it during workout sessions.
2. **Visual aids for past workout statistics.** Add visualizations of saved workout
   history so users can understand progress over time. This follows basic history
   viewing because the app first needs reliable workout records. Advanced visuals
   are deferred from the MVP, which provides the underlying logs. Contributors
   can help identify useful statistics and build and test their visualizations.

## Later

These P2 features are exploratory ideas from the project proposal. They follow the
MVP and P1 improvements because they expand the app from recording user-created
plans into suggesting plans and starting workouts without an exiting plan, requiring additional design and validation.

1. **Generate one-off workouts or workout plans.** Help users assemble a one-off workouts
   rather than requiring them to create or select a plan. Generated workouts can then be saved as a new template if desired. This is
   deferred until the exercise catalog and template workflows are established.
   Contributors can help define generation rules and check that generated plans
   use the catalog and fit the existing template model.
2. **Suggest workouts for fitness goals or sports training.** Explore suggestions
   tailored to a user's stated goal or sport. This is deferred because the proposal
   identifies a need for more evidence about what users want from planning.
   Contributors can help research those needs, define the supported goals, and
   evaluate suggestions before implementation.

## Not planned

These non-goals from the proposal remain outside the current plan. They are
excluded to protect the semester scope and the focus on individual workout
planning and logging.

- **Nutrition or macro tracking.** This introduces a separate problem area and
  would stretch the project beyond the available build time.
- **Body composition and fitness goal customization.** Automatically prescribing
  workouts, repetitions, or weights using body-profile information such as gender,
  height, and weight is outside the semester scope. The exploratory goal- or
  sport-based suggestions in Later do not commit the project to this broader
  personalization system.
- **Social exercising features.** Friends, followers, workout sharing, comments,
  and cooperative workout logging are excluded because the project prioritizes
  meeting individual users' needs independently.
# LibreLift - Design Document

|                  |                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Authors**      | James Teuscher                                                                                                                                            |
| **Reviewers**    | [who reviewed it — a teammate, the instructor, a design-review partner]                                                                                   |
| **Status**       | In review                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Last updated** | 11-17-26                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Links**        | [proposal](../cp3/cp3-proposal) · [repository](https://github.com/LibreLift/expo_suite) · [issue tracker](https://github.com/LibreLift/expo_suite/issues) |

## Revision history

| Date     | Author         | What changed                   |
| -------- | -------------- | ------------------------------ |
| 10-16-26 | James Teuscher | First draft                    |
| 10-20-26 | James Teuscher | First full draft               |
| 10-21-26 | James Teuscher | Finished first copy            |
| 11-4-26  | James Teuscher | Revised to respond to feedback |
| 11-9-26  | Codex | Record frontend decisions and clarify shared terminology |
| 11-17-26 | Codex | Record the confirmed M1 database scope and account-name ownership |

---

## 1. Context and scope

LibreLift is a native mobile app for planning, logging, and tracking workouts for those who want to use their phones to do so. It aims to provide the basic functions of creating reusable workout templates, using a template for a workout and logging reps and weight, and reviewing the details of past workouts. For more information about the context of this project, see the [proposal document](../cp3/cp3-proposal).

Use the [glossary](../GLOSSARY.md) for canonical domain terms. The
[architecture decision records](./adr/README.md) and
[UI foundation decision summary](./ui-foundation.md) explain the frontend choices
recorded during #38.

## 2. Goals and non-goals

**Goals**

- Connect to RepDB, an external exercise DB, and load its free exercise catalog into the app for use. Besides name, the exercises in the app should be identifiable by target muscles and equipment.
- Support creation, persistence, editing, and deletion of reusable workout templates.
- Support starting, stopping, and completing workout sessions for an existing template. Workout sessions allow recording repetitions performed and weight used for each session exercise.
- Support storing "one-rep" maximum weight for certain exercises, and enter weight in template exercises as a percentage of that maximum.

**Non-goals**

- Social exercising features such as followers/friends, sharing workouts, leaving comments, etc., are excluded. They fall outside the scope of primary user needs.
- No body composition and fitness goal customization. 

## 3. System-context diagram

There will only be one type of user interacting with this system. They will create workout templates and record workout sessions. The CDN/API that provides a catalog of exercises will interact with the system by providing the exercise catalog via HTTP. Lastly, Supabase will interact with the system by providing the authentication service, database and data access layer, and serverless backend to handle HTTP requests for auth and data access.

![diagram](./design-images/system-context-diagram.jpg)

## 4. Architecture and components

| Component      | Responsibility                                                                   | Talks to                            | Interface (rough)                     |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| View           | Displays UI and accepts user input                                               | ViewModel                           | function calls, touch screen elements |
| ViewModel      | Business logic of logging, templating, and weight calculation                    | View, Service                       | function calls                        |
| Service        | Makes calls to backend to read/write data for ViewModel operations               | ViewModel, HTTPHandlers             | function calls, HTTP                  |
| HTTPHandlers   | Accepts incoming HTTP calls from frontend, handles request payloads              | Service, DataAccess, Authentication | function calls, HTTP                  |
| Authentication | Accepts authentication requests via HTTP, uses Supabase auth to accept or reject | HTTPHandler                         | function calls, HTTP                  |
| DataAccess     | Adjusts HTTP payloads to be ready for DB reads/writes                            | DB, HTTPHandlers                    | function calls, HTTP                  |
| DB             | Stores data persistently, supplies data for app UI                               | DataAccess                          | HTTP                                  |

![component diagram](./design-images/component-diagram.JPG)

### Initial frontend foundation (#38)

The Expo/TypeScript frontend follows MVVM: View components render hooks in the
ViewModel layer, which depend on an injected asynchronous `WorkoutService`.
The root layout originally supplied a sample implementation; the #45 persistence
integration below now supplies production template operations. Template targets and historical session values are separate snapshots.

Expo Router provides three bottom tabs: Templates (initial), Workouts, and Account.
Templates have a saved overview listing exercise names and set counts. Each
placement opens saved exercise detail with its preserved image (or an unavailable
placeholder) and compact read-only set rows. Saved detail reads the template
snapshot without loading the catalog. The complete draft editor manages name,
optional description, catalog exercise placements, and independent fixed-weight
sets.
Editing uses a template overview for name/description, exercise count, membership,
and order, plus a separate screen for one placement’s sets and targets. Each set
is one row: Set number, reps input, ×, weight input, and pounds. Back/Done from
exercise editing returns to the overview without committing; both screens share
one draft, and Save/Cancel on the overview applies to all changes. The overview's
Sets button sits beside the exercise title and trash control. Saved targets and
editable targets use the same row layout; only the editor exposes numeric inputs
and set removal.
Creation, whole-template updates, and deletion use the injected asynchronous
WorkoutService backed by memory. New templates append to the list. Successful
mutations invalidate list/detail reads and refresh counts. A fresh app session
restored the two samples. The #45 integration below supersedes that production
composition; controlled in-memory services remain test doubles.

The root owns the service and shared draft state, allowing catalog selection to
return to the same draft. Repeated catalog exercises have independent placement
identities and snapshots. The builder supports long-press dragging from an
edit-only three-line handle, scrolling while dragging, and accessible Move up/down
alternatives. All targets move with their placement. Existing history remains
independent of template edits/deletions.

Save validates and commits the whole draft atomically. Failed saves preserve it
for retry. Tabs preserve unfinished drafts; Back/swipe offers discard/keep editing.
Save/Cancel applies to the entire draft. Pending saves/deletes lock conflicting
actions and navigation. Delete requires confirmation naming the template and
returns to the list on success. See the [confirmed #91 specification](./issue-91-template-crud.md)
for target validation, lifecycle, and testing decisions.

Workout history has independently collapsible exercise sections. Account displays
the application User's name and Auth account's email, offers name editing, and
links to Settings. Email-code account access gates training; workout logging
remains a feature integration.

Settings offers Light, Dark, and System appearance, defaulting to System. The
preference is stored locally through an injected storage interface. Both themes
use the [selected palette](https://colorhunt.co/palette/2c36393f4e4fa27b5cdcd7c9)
with additional neutral colors for readability. Sample weights use pounds.

The app uses SDK 58 to match the Expo Go version installed on the review device.
See [setup](./setup.md) for compatibility and device review instructions.

### Authentication session lifecycle (#43)

Stored Supabase authentication is restored before protected navigation mounts,
then the application User is loaded using the existing name/onboarding contract.
No application lifetime or inactivity timeout is imposed. The SDK owns persisted
credentials and refresh; protected operations use its current identity.

Routine same-account token refresh preserves drafts and navigation. Unusable
access gates training; retryable failures preserve stored credentials and offer
Retry, Sign out, and appearance Settings. Recovery starts a clean account load
and discards unsaved work/navigation with an explanation. Definitively ended
authentication returns to email access. Native foreground/background handling
starts/stops SDK auto-refresh and checks expired access on return.

Device-local sign-out confirms unsaved changes, is disabled during saves, and
succeeds locally despite server revocation failure. Local storage cleanup failure
instead gates access behind Retry sign-out. Forced loss overrides pending guards.
An account-generation boundary resets account-specific services, providers,
drafts, cached reads, edits, and navigation, while late results cannot restore
old state. Appearance preferences and saved backend records remain. Future
maximums state must share this lifecycle; its concrete verification remains #49.
See [the confirmed #43 specification](issue-43-auth-sessions.md).

### Exercise catalog boundary (#44)

RepDB JSON is validated at the service boundary into a shared catalog exercise
model with a namespaced catalog identifier, English name, separate primary and
secondary muscles, and explicit equipment requirements. Optional images,
instructions, and German/Spanish content are retained in the model.
Usable records are returned with diagnostics for malformed data; an unusable
response has a distinct failure result.

The #83 implementation adds a temporary standalone catalog screen opened from
Templates. A separately injected catalog service receives an HTTP request
function and loads the single JSON document at
`https://exercise-dataset.com/exercises.json`, using the existing mapper. The
ViewModel exposes loading, usable results, and defined transport/response failure
states. A virtualized list shows exercises alphabetically with colloquial muscle
groups and equipment. Primary and secondary groups remain separate; raw muscles
remain unchanged in the model. Rejected records produce a quiet partial-results
notice; optional-content diagnostics alone do not. Each visit loads afresh,
retaining results while open, with Back available on failure. Caching, retries,
and adding or saving exercises in the template editor remain separate work.
The #84 implementation combines case-insensitive exercise-name search with one
primary muscle-group filter, defaulting to All muscles. Secondary targets never
cause filter matches. No-match results offer Clear search and filter without
another request. Search/filter state survives tab changes while the route stays
open and resets on leaving and reopening. The catalog and README credit RepDB.
See [the agreed catalog behavior](./issue-53-exercise-catalog.md).

Tapping a catalog card opens an image-first detail screen using the selected
record from that visit. Start/peak images are swipeable, labeled pages with
Previous/Next controls; single illustrations use the same uncropped image area.
Images have independent loading/failure states. Group summaries, equipment, and
numbered English instructions follow the images. The mounted list retains its
scroll position and controls beneath detail without another JSON request.
The selected record is released when the catalog list unmounts. A detail route
without it offers Open catalog. See [the confirmed detail behavior](./catalog-exercise-detail.md).

Template exercises and session exercises each have their own placement identity
and copy descriptive exercise details and sets, retaining the shared catalog
identity. Upstream catalog changes cannot alter saved templates or history.
See the [catalog contract and tracking](./issue-44-exercise-catalog.md) and
[identity decision](./adr/issue-44-catalog-identity-and-snapshots.md).

### Core flow - Making a workout template

1. A user logs in or signs up with credentials
2. User taps the screen to create a workout template
3. View layer sends input to ViewModel
4. ViewModel navigates to template creator business logic, calls service to load catalog
5. Service calls the Exercise CDN to load catalog, returns data to ViewModel
6. ViewModel sends exercises to View
7. View displays exercises
8. User chooses exercises, weight, reps
9. View sends selections to ViewModel
10. ViewModel saves the workout template in-memory as the user builds it
11. User taps "Save plan"
12. View call ViewModel's save function
13. ViewModel sends workout template data to service via function call
14. Service serializes the workout template into JSON, calls backend via HTTP
15. HTTPHandler receives workout template JSON, passes to DataAccess layer via function call
16. DataAccess layer deserializes JSON, writes to DB via HTTP

### The failure case

1. User taps the screen to create a workout template
2. View layer sends input to ViewModel
3. ViewModel navigates to template creator business logic, calls service to load catalog
4. Service checks if the catalog is cached. If not, call the Service layer
5. Service calls the Exercise CDN to load catalog, returns data to ViewModel
6. CDN throws an error and does not return catalog
7. Service passes an error to the ViewModel layer
8. ViewModel layer formats the error message to display on the UI
9. UI displays the error message for the User, asks to wait for a period and then try again

### Core flow - Logging a workout:

1. A user logs in using credentials
2. User selects one of their templates and taps  a "Start workout" button.
3. A stopwatch/counter displays workout duration, and lists the exercises in the workout.
4. For each exercise, the user is able to tap it and see a detailed view 
5. The user can adjust actual weight and reps used if it differs from the templated amounts
6. After performing a set of one exercise, the user marks that set complete.
7. This is repeated for the planned sets of each exercise; the MVP does not group exercises into circuit rounds.
8. When finished, the user taps "Finish workout"
9. The workout session is completed and added to the user's workout history
10. The user can navigate to workout history and see the details of their session

### The failure case

1. A user logs in using credentials
2. User selects one of their templates and taps  a "Start workout" button.
3. The user proceeds through the workout as stated above
4. When tapping the "Finish workout" button, the DB write fails
5. The error message is sent back to the user and told to try again in a few minutes.
6. If the error persists a second time, the user is presented a button to send feedback.
7. The feedback link sends an email to the maintainers with the user input.

## 5. Data model

| Entity            | Key fields                                                                             | Relationships                                                             | MVP or roadmap |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| User              | id, account_name                                                                       | has workout templates, has workout sessions, and has exercise max weights | MVP            |
| Exercise          | exercise_id, name, muscles, equipmenet                                                 | has a User max weight, part of template exercise and session exercise     | MVP            |
| Workout template  | userId, template_id, title                                                             | belongs to User, has exercises, fills a workout session                   | MVP            |
| Template exercise | template_exercise_id, exercise_id, template_id, position                               | part of Workout template, is an exercise, has sets                        | MVP            |
| Template set      | template_exercise_id, set_number, target_weight, target_reps                           | part of Template exercise                                                 | MVP            |
| User exercise max | user_id, exercise_id, max_weight                                                       | belongs to User, describes exercise                                       | MVP            |
| Workout session   | session_id, user_id, template_id, start_time, end_time                                 | belongs to user, filled by workout template, contains session exercises   | MVP            |
| Session exercise  | session_exercise_id, session_id, exercise_id, position                                 | part of Workout session, has session sets                                 | MVP            |
| Session sets      | sesson_exercise_id, set_number, target_weight, target_reps, actual_weight, actual_reps | part of session workout                                                   | MVP            |

### M1 database scope and account data (#102)

See the [confirmed #102 specification](./issue-102-database.md) for acceptance
criteria, implementation boundaries, and the approved database testing seam.

The M1 database includes an application-owned User table, workout templates,
template exercises, and template sets. Workout sessions, session exercises,
session sets, personal exercise maximums, and percentage-based targets are added
through later migrations for M2; the table above describes the broader MVP model.

The application-owned User table stores the editable account name and uses the
Supabase Auth account's ID as its identity. Training records reference this
application User for ownership and relationships. The account name is a display
name, not a unique sign-in identifier. This decision replaces #42's use of Auth
user metadata for the account name. Do not add application columns to or otherwise
alter Supabase's managed Auth schema; Supabase Auth continues to manage credentials
and authentication sessions.

After email verification, an authenticated account-data read loads the application
User if one exists. An absent User requires name onboarding without creating a
row. Submitting a valid account name creates the User with the Auth account's ID;
a failed save preserves the entered name for retry. Existing Users load their
stored account name. Account access integration in #42 must follow this flow.

If email-code verification succeeds but the application User lookup fails, retain
the verified authentication session in memory and keep training screens gated.
Show an actionable error with **Retry loading account**, which retries only the
User lookup, without requesting or verifying another code. Appearance Settings
remains available. Only a successful lookup with no User opens name onboarding;
a lookup failure remains in the retry state. This recovery is part of #42;
authentication restoration and lifecycle are specified below.

Template exercises store their placement identity, namespaced catalog identity,
parent template, and position relationally. Each placement also stores a complete
descriptive JSON snapshot, including name, distinct primary and secondary muscles,
equipment, and available images, instructions, and translations. Template sets
remain relational. Saved detail reads these snapshots without consulting the live
catalog; #102 does not import a shared exercise catalog table. This implements the
existing catalog identity and snapshot decision rather than treating the ERD's
Exercise entity as a live source of saved descriptions.

Authenticated database requests use the requesting account's context so row-level
security applies. Explicit grants and policies allow only owner-scoped access to
application User and template data; anonymous access is denied. Backend operations
must not routinely bypass these policies with a privileged service credential.
Deleting a template cascades to its placements and sets. Deleting an Auth account
cascades to its application User and owned templates. Users cannot change their
identity or transfer ownership. An account-deletion UI remains outside M1 scope.

Saved templates and template-exercise placements use UUID identities. Placement
identity remains unchanged when exercises move; a separate numeric position
records order. Template sets use numbers within their placement. Templates store
creation timestamps for stable list ordering. Draft identity conversion belongs
to #45's persistence integration.

Database constraints enforce valid relationships, nonblank names, nonnegative
finite decimal weights in pounds, positive integer target repetitions, and unique
exercise positions and set numbers within their parents. Issue #45 validates and
saves a complete template atomically, including at least one exercise, at least
one set per exercise, and consecutive ordering. Multirow edits may temporarily
have incomplete structure within their transaction.

Issue #102's primary verification seam is the real local Supabase database, using
anonymous and two authenticated identities. Tests verify allowed operations,
ownership isolation and attempted ownership changes, invalid values, snapshots,
ordering, and deletion cascades. Migrations must rebuild cleanly and apply to a
populated database without losing existing records. App-flow verification remains
with #42 and #45. Deliver locally verified migrations and hosted deployment
instructions; applying them to the shared hosted backend follows the existing
post-review maintainer workflow. Do not automatically seed user data or sample
templates.

Issue #102 owns the M1 schema, relationship constraints, access grants, row-level
security, and database verification. Issue #45 builds template persistence
operations and app integration on that foundation; #43 owns authentication-session
restoration. Valid stored authentication is restored automatically, while explicit
sign-out or an app reinstall requires another email OTP. Saved templates belong
to the account and survive app reloads, restarts, updates, and reinstalls when
using the same backend. Unsaved template drafts remain temporary.

### Template persistence (#45)

The [confirmed #45 specification](./issue-45-template-persistence.md) governs the
implemented production template service; hosted deployment and device audit remain
separate review activities. Whole-template
saves use an authenticated Edge Function/data-access boundary and an invoker-rights
transactional database function; see [ADR 0005](./adr/0005-save-template-aggregates-transactionally.md).
An unchanged save retry recovers its original committed result without duplicate
creation or overwriting later saves. Distinct concurrent saves use last-committed
whole-template replacement; updates never recreate deleted templates, and deletion
of an absent template succeeds. Production accounts receive no sample templates;
workout history remains visibly labeled sample data until #47. The approved tests
combine existing router-level behavior checks with the real production service
through HTTP to disposable local Supabase. The root shares one lazy authenticated
client and injects Expo Crypto UUID generation into its account-scoped service.
Every production request checks its account and pins that session's bearer token;
a switched account cannot reuse an older service. A guarded refresh retries a
rejected current token once. Definitive loss enters existing account recovery,
scoped by account identity and generation so late failures cannot clear a new
account. Ordinary permission/transport errors preserve the draft. See the
[validation record](./issue-125-template-production.md) and setup commands.

**ERD:**
![Entity-Relationship Diagram](./design-images/librelift-erd.jpg)


## 6. Technology choices and alternatives considered

### Decision: What ExerciseDB/CDN will be used

- **Chosen:** RepDB
- **Alternative considered:** yuhonas/free-exercise-db
- **Why the chosen option wins, given our goals:** There is a free starter license, and the example images are superior than those in free-exercise-db
- **Evidence:** The spike utilized RepDB, while a personal side project has utilized free-exercise-db, and the RepDB images are superior, while muscle grouping, exercises available, and instructions are roughly equivalent.
- **What would change our mind:** If the user base grows enough that the RepDB free license is no longer usable, I would want to switch to the free alternative of free-exercise-db
### Decision: Which Backend as a Service (BaaS) technology will be used?

- **Chosen**: Supabase
- **Alternative considered**: Firebase
- **Why the chosen option wins, given our goals**: 2 main reasons: First, Supabase is better build for open-source contributions, since contributors can run a local version of the backend without needing access to the production credentials. Second, the data model for LibreLift (workouts, exercises, template vs session) fits well in a relational model, which is more readily available in Supabase. One advantage that Firebase does have is out of the box support for offline-synchronization.
- **Evidence**: The Supabase CLI allows any developer to run backend services locally with one command (`npx supabase start`). This is a huge asset for an open-source project. Supabase is naturally relational with PostgreSQL, and Firebase is natively NoSQL. Firebase does support SQL using SQL Connect, which requires some additional configuration. Offline synchronization is possible with Supabase, but requires more manual configuration than Firebase.
- **What would change our mind**: If offline synchronization became too complex with Supabase, switching to Firebase would become a real consideration. Or, if the scale of the project grows enough and pricing between Supabase and Firebase favor Firebase, that would also merit considering a switch.

### Decision: What authentication method will be used

**Chosen**: Email OTP only.
**Alternatives considered**: Email + password, email magic link, Google OAuth, Apple OAuth.
**Why the chosen option wins, given our goals**: Users are expected to sign in infrequently and remain signed in on their device. Email OTP avoids managing a rarely used password and the configuration overhead of OAuth providers.
**Evidence**: Supabase supports email OTP for new and returning users and renewable sessions without a default maximum lifetime. During the Issue #42 design discussion, this approach was selected based on the expected infrequency of sign-ins for a gym app. The expectation is that users will sign in once and then use the app as desired.
**What would change our mind**: Evidence that users need another sign-in method.

See [ADR 0004: Use email OTP for account access](./adr/0004-email-otp-account-access.md)
for the agreed account-access behavior, session boundary, and testing decisions.

## 7. Risks and open questions

| Risk or question                                                                                                          | Why it matters                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Owner | How we'll find out, and by when                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| How precisely to represent workout and exercise templates vs workout and exercise sessions/completions in the data model? | Doing so inefficiently can erode DB performance, and add unnecessary overhead to the Data Access component                                                                                                      | James | Do research during M1, determine the ideal data model                                                 |
| How to provision Supabase Edge functions and DB                                                                           | This is where all of the data storage and backend computing will live. Without this, the app does not provide value.                                                                                            | James | Read Supabase docs and run through quick starts for DB and Edge functions during  M1                  |
| How to distribute to iOS devices without the $99/year developer profile fee?                                              | Purchasing the developer profile would significantly increase the cost of the project. But, iOS is a major mobile OS that cannot be simply neglected, but must be supported                                     | James | Research distribution methods during M1 and M2, select a long-term solution with a fallback plan.     |
| RepDB's Starter license has limited terms                                                                                 | Misunderstanding the limits could lead to legal liability, necessity to purchase their expensive paid license, or pivot to another exercise catalog                                                             | James | Determine and document limits of free version of license during M2, before public demo and release    |
| Will workouts be lost if the final save fails?                                                                            | Some gyms have spotty wifi, so the final save to the DB failing is a very real possibility. Users losing their logged progress due to this would be a major failure in one of the primary intentions of the app | James | During M2, research methods to backup copies of the workout session and recover if the DB write fails |

## 8. Implementation plan

| Milestone | What works when it's done                                                                                                                     | Depends on | Build hours (estimate) |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------------------- |
| 1         | The first core flow (template creation) works, without "one-rep" maximum support. Editing and deleting templates is also supported.           | —          | 12                     |
| 2         | Both core flows (template creation and workout sessions) work and  support "one-rep" maximum recording and calculations based off that value. | 1          | 8                      |

# Use MVVM with injected asynchronous services

For [#38](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues/38), UI stubs need to behave
like clients of real data while backend features are still being built. Views
therefore render ViewModel state, and ViewModels consume injected asynchronous
service interfaces; the app's root supplies sample data and preference-storage
implementations. This adds a small amount of boundary code compared with embedding
fixtures in screens, but allows service integration and controlled failure testing
without coupling the views to either fixtures or backend clients.
# Preserve session history independently of templates

The [roadmap](../roadmap.md#mvp) requires template edits and reuse to leave earlier
workout sessions unchanged. Session exercises, target performance, and recorded
performance therefore belong to the session independently of the editable
template, accepting duplicated values instead of reconstructing history from the
current template. The current sample records demonstrate this separation; session
creation and backend persistence remain future feature work.
# Separate exercise placements from catalog identity and preserve saved details

Template and session exercise placements have their own identifiers while retaining the same catalog identifier for the movement they reference. Saved templates and sessions preserve exercise details rather than resolving them from the current external catalog, so repeated placements remain distinct and upstream renames or removals cannot alter saved workouts. This accepts duplicated descriptive data in exchange for stable saved plans and history.

Catalog identifiers include a provider namespace, such as `repdb:bench-press`, to prevent accidental identity collisions if another catalog is introduced. Equivalent movements from different providers require an explicit mapping; matching names or provider-local identifiers do not establish equivalence.

{"body":"> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

**Goal**:

A signed-in user can reopen their account without another email code, and ending or changing authentication prevents the next user from seeing the previous account's data.

**Context**:

Part of #40. Replaces session/authentication integration from #25 and account/session types from #24. Implementation: agent. Supports M1: Runnable Demo. This specification records the maintainer-confirmed design discussion and approved testing seams.

Prerequisites #38, #39, #41, and #42 are closed. There are no sub-issues. Downstream tasks #45, #47, and #49 consume this authentication lifecycle. #102 owns the application User/template database foundation; #42 established application User/name integration and the current-run account-access gate.

## Problem Statement

LibreLift stores Supabase credentials on the device but does not restore them into application state when the app launches. Returning users must repeat account access, and the app does not yet respond to session lifecycle changes or provide sign-out.

Training services, cached reads, and unfinished work can outlive protected routes. Simply returning to email entry would therefore leave the previous account's state available in memory. Users need reliable returning access and a clear boundary that prevents one account's state from appearing under another account.

## Solution

Restore usable stored authentication behind a loading gate, load the application User, and enter the app only after any required account-name onboarding. Keep sessions renewable without an application-imposed maximum lifetime or inactivity timeout.

Routine same-account token refresh preserves ongoing work. When authentication becomes unusable, gate training. Temporary failures offer recovery without erasing stored authentication; successful recovery starts with a clean load and discards drafts and navigation. Definitively invalid authentication clears account-specific state and returns to email access.

Provide device-local sign-out. Clear account-specific services, caches, edits, drafts, and navigation when authentication ends or the account changes, and prevent late responses from repopulating them. Preserve device appearance preferences and saved backend data.

## User Stories

1. As a returning user, I want valid stored authentication restored when I launch the app, so that I do not need another email code.
2. As a user, I want a loading screen while restoration is unresolved, so that I understand why training is not yet available.
3. As a user of a shared device, I want protected content hidden during restoration, so that another account's information is never briefly displayed.
4. As a user without stored authentication, I want to reach email account access, so that I can sign in.
5. As a returning user, I want expired access credentials renewed when possible, so that ordinary access-token expiry does not require email verification.
6. As a signed-in user, I want routine background token refresh to preserve my draft and current screen, so that maintenance of authentication does not interrupt editing.
7. As a returning user, I want my application User loaded before training opens, so that account readiness is established.
8. As a verified user without an application User/account name, I want name onboarding, so that I can complete account setup.
9. As a user whose account lookup fails, I want account-loading retry rather than name onboarding, so that a failure is not mistaken for a missing User.
10. As a user facing a temporary restoration failure, I want Retry without losing stored authentication, so that I can recover without another email code.
11. As a user facing an authentication outage, I want appearance Settings available, so that recovery does not prevent adjusting the display.
12. As a user facing a recovery screen, I want Sign out available, so that I can abandon the stored account.
13. As a signed-in user whose authentication becomes unusable, I want training gated, so that protected actions are not offered without usable authentication.
14. As a user recovering from unusable authentication, I want a clean reload, so that I re-enter a consistent account state.
15. As a user whose recovery discards an unsaved draft, I want that loss explained, so that the reset is understandable.
16. As a user whose credentials are definitively invalid, I want to return to email access with an explanation, so that I know how to continue.
17. As a user returning from the background, I want authentication lifecycle handling to resume, so that expired or ended access is handled correctly.
18. As a signed-in user, I want Sign out on Account, so that I can end access on this device.
19. As a user signing out, I want my other devices to remain signed in, so that a local action does not interrupt them.
20. As a user without unsaved changes, I want sign-out without an unnecessary confirmation, so that the action is straightforward.
21. As a user with unsaved changes, I want a discard warning before deliberate sign-out, so that I can keep editing instead.
22. As a user who confirms sign-out, I want unsaved changes discarded, so that they cannot appear for the next account.
23. As a user with a pending save, I want deliberate sign-out disabled until the operation settles, so that conflicting actions do not overlap.
24. As a user whose authentication ends during a save, I want protected content removed immediately, so that a pending operation cannot hold the account open.
25. As a user signing out while offline, I want local access and stored credentials cleared even if server revocation fails, so that the next person cannot reopen my account.
26. As a user whose device credential cleanup fails, I want a blocking error and Retry, so that the app does not falsely claim sign-out succeeded.
27. As a user whose cleanup is unresolved, I want protected access and another account's entry blocked, so that identities cannot become mixed.
28. As a user stuck in name onboarding or account loading, I want Sign out available, so that I can leave that account.
29. As a user switching accounts, I want to sign out and continue with another email, so that I can use the intended account.
30. As a user entering a different account, I want the previous account's templates, history, drafts, and account edits absent, so that I see only the current account state.
31. As a user signing back into the same account after sign-out, I want fresh in-memory state, so that abandoned work is not resurrected.
32. As a user, I want late responses from an earlier account or ended access period ignored, so that they cannot replace current data or change navigation.
33. As a user, I want Back navigation unable to reopen the previous account's screens, so that sign-out actually ends visible access.
34. As a user launching normally or completing account access, I want Templates to open after the gates pass, so that I have a predictable starting point.
35. As a user opening a valid protected direct link, I want access checks and onboarding completed first, so that direct navigation cannot bypass protection.
36. As a user, I want protected requests to use the current account's credentials, so that data operations run under the correct identity.
37. As a user, I want saved backend data retained when I sign out, so that ending device access does not delete my training records.
38. As a user of a shared device, I want the device appearance preference retained through account changes, so that the display remains comfortable.
39. As a user of either supported mobile platform, I want readable loading, recovery, confirmation, and sign-out controls, so that I can manage access on my device.

## Implementation Decisions

- Extend the existing injected asynchronous authentication service and auth ViewModel/provider to support stored-session restoration, lifecycle updates, recovery, and local sign-out. Continue the MVVM boundary: views render state, services hide Supabase details, and SDK credentials are not exposed to View components.
- Reuse the shared Supabase client and existing persisted-session storage/process lock. Let the SDK manage token renewal; do not create a competing refresh-token store or independent renewal loop. Handle native foreground/background lifecycle and dispose listeners/subscriptions appropriately.
- Represent unresolved restoration separately from signed-out access. Gate protected routes, including direct entry, until usable authentication and application User loading/name onboarding are resolved. Do not briefly render cached training or prematurely show email entry during a valid restoration.
- Restoration reuses the existing application User contract: load the account's User; an absent User requires name onboarding; a failed lookup remains a retryable loading failure. Auth metadata is not the authoritative account name. Do not create an application User merely by restoring credentials.
- Distinguish an expired access token that can be renewed from definitively ended authentication. Retain the ADR's renewable-session intent and impose no maximum lifetime or inactivity timeout.
- Routine same-account background token refresh updates current credentials without resetting drafts, cached training, or navigation. Repeated same-account lifecycle notifications alone must not be treated as account changes.
- When authentication becomes unusable, immediately gate training and prevent protected actions. A temporary network/service failure preserves stored authentication and offers Retry, Sign out, and appearance Settings. Do not require another OTP solely because a retryable service failure occurred.
- Successful recovery after authentication became unusable starts a clean account load: discard unsaved drafts, account edits, account-specific cached data, and prior protected navigation before training reopens. Explain draft loss. This reset also applies if recovery returns the same account. It does not apply to routine token refresh while authentication remains usable.
- Definitive credential invalidation or a signed-out transition clears account-specific state and returns to email entry with an explanation. Classify authentication failure separately from ordinary network, application validation, or permission errors; an arbitrary failed protected request is not proof that the whole authentication session ended.
- Define an account-lifetime boundary around both stateful service instances and their providers/resources. Reset template drafts, mutated sample-service data, list/detail reads, workout history state, account edits, pending-operation state, catalog selections associated with drafts, and protected navigation when authentication ends or identity changes. Unmounting screen components alone is insufficient because the existing root-owned sample service and draft provider survive route changes.
- Invalidate outstanding work at that boundary. Late restoration results, User loads, name updates, training reads/writes, and old auth updates cannot overwrite newer account state or trigger stale navigation. This includes sign-out followed by sign-in to the same account.
- Forced authentication loss takes priority over pending-operation and unsaved-navigation guards. Immediately hide protected content and perform cleanup. A backend request already accepted may still commit; client cleanup does not promise rollback or deletion of saved records.
- Deliberate sign-out is disabled while a save is pending. Otherwise, ask for confirmation only when unsaved changes exist; cancel preserves work and confirmed sign-out discards it. Apply pending controls to prevent duplicate sign-out/recovery actions.
- Sign out only the current device session, explicitly selecting local scope rather than the SDK's global default. Remove local stored credentials and account state and return to email entry even if the best-effort server revocation request fails. Do not claim all devices were signed out, server revocation succeeded on failure, or already issued access tokens were immediately invalidated.
- Local credential-cleanup failure is different from server revocation failure. Keep protected content hidden, show a blocking cleanup error with Retry, and prevent another account from entering until durable local cleanup succeeds. Do not report successful sign-out while stored authentication can still be restored.
- Offer Sign out on Account, name onboarding, and authentication/account recovery screens. Preserve appearance Settings and device appearance preferences across authentication transitions.
- Ordinary restored launch, successful sign-in, and clean recovery open Templates after account readiness. Valid protected direct links wait for authentication and required onboarding. Prior protected navigation is not restored after a clean recovery or account change. Back cannot expose ended account access or the previous account's protected screens.
- Account switching is sign-out followed by the existing email OTP flow. Do not add a multi-account picker.
- Protected service requests use the shared client's current authenticated context, including refreshed credentials. Do not use an account ID or publishable key as proof of user identity, capture a stale UI token for later requests, or introduce privileged credentials into the app. Feature backends must preserve that requesting-user context so ownership policies apply.
- Existing application User operations provide a real protected request path for this issue. Template, workout-session, and maximum persistence/backends remain with #45, #47, and #49; authentication lifecycle work does not require implementing them here.
- No personal exercise maximum state currently exists. Amend the original seeded-maximum acceptance expectation: #43 proves cleanup of existing template/history/draft state and establishes the lifecycle future maximum state must share; concrete maximums cleanup verification belongs to #49. Do not build a maximum model/cache solely for this test.
- No database schema change is required for this specification. Saved backend data survives local cleanup and sign-out. Keep existing email OTP behavior, application User storage, appearance behavior, and supported mobile environments.

## Testing Decisions

- The maintainer approved the existing router-level seam as the primary boundary: mount real screens/navigation with injected authentication and workout services, controlled clocks, and deferred asynchronous results.
- Good tests assert visible content, available actions, navigation, and externally observable service behavior. Avoid tests coupled to hook internals, provider layout, implementation call order, or incidental SDK event counts.
- Extend existing account-access/navigation tests and their controlled service doubles. Existing template draft, pending-save, error/retry, and history navigation tests provide prior art for seeded state and delayed outcomes.
- Cover valid restoration, no stored session, pending restoration without a protected-content or sign-in flash, expired-but-renewable access, definitive invalidation, missing User/name onboarding, and failed User lookup/retry.
- Cover routine same-account refresh preserving draft and navigation; temporary unusable authentication gating training; retry without another OTP; and successful recovery performing a clean load with draft/navigation loss.
- Cover local sign-out with and without unsaved changes, cancel/confirm behavior, deliberate sign-out disabled during pending saves, forced loss overriding pending guards, and sign-out available from onboarding/recovery.
- Cover server revocation failure with successful local sign-out separately from device storage cleanup failure with blocked access and retry. Verify successful cleanup prevents restoration on a subsequent launch.
- Seed distinct existing template/history/draft/account-edit state. Verify sign-out, account change, and signing back into the same account do not resurrect it. Appearance preferences must remain.
- Resolve old account/restoration/name/training operations after sign-out, identity change, or recovery and assert they neither repopulate data nor navigate. Verify Back and protected direct links obey the gate.
- Supplement the primary UI seam with the existing disposable-local-Supabase verification approach. Exercise actual persisted restoration across service recreation, renewal, local sign-out, restart after sign-out, and protected application User requests under two accounts/current credentials. Verify local sign-out leaves a separate device/session usable.
- Feature-specific persistence and actual cross-account database isolation remain tested in their owning tasks. Concrete maximums cleanup belongs to #49.
- During implementation, run the checked-in TypeScript and Jest commands and appropriate native bundle/dependency checks. Device review must cover process restart, foreground/background lifecycle, sign-out/re-entry, protected-content gating, readable recovery controls, and both themes. Physical iPhone with Expo Go is the first review target; Android remains supported. Automated tests and bundles do not replace native review.

## Out of Scope

- Implementing template, workout-session/history, or personal exercise maximum persistence, feature HTTP endpoints, or feature-specific ownership policies.
- Adding a maximum model/cache or maximum screens merely to satisfy cleanup coverage.
- Offline training, offline synchronization, draft persistence, or recovering unsaved work after unusable authentication recovers.
- A multi-account picker, sign-out-all-devices UI, account deletion, sign-in email changes, or new profile fields.
- Passwords, password recovery, OAuth, magic links, authentication callbacks, or changing the agreed email OTP flow.
- New app-imposed session lifetime/inactivity limits, replacement credential storage architecture, or immediate invalidation of already issued access tokens.
- Deleting saved backend training data on sign-out or promising rollback of a request already accepted by the backend.

**Goal**: A signed-in user can save, reload, edit, reorder, and delete complete workout templates that remain private to their account and survive app lifecycles.

**Context**: Part of #32. Replaces the template-data portion of #24 and template backend work from #25. Supports M1: Runnable Demo. Implementation: agent. Builds on #39, #43, #44, and #102; all four are closed. Authentication lifecycle prerequisite #43 was delivered by merged PR #118. The existing #91 template editor is the frontend baseline. The maintainer approved the decisions and testing seams below during the specification discussion.

**Acceptance criteria**:

- [ ] Production template CRUD uses the injected service, authenticated HTTP/Edge Function, data-access boundary, and real database; new accounts receive an empty template list rather than seeded samples.
- [ ] Complete templates round-trip with UUID identities, immutable creation timestamps, deterministic listing, ordered independent placements, complete exercise snapshots, and numbered fixed-weight sets.
- [ ] Whole-template validation and writes are atomic, including placement removal/addition/reordering, with no partial commit on failure.
- [ ] Retrying an unchanged save after a lost response returns its original saved result without duplicate creation or overwriting a later save; editing the retained draft makes a new save attempt against the same template identity.
- [ ] The last committed distinct whole-template save wins; updates never recreate deleted templates, and deleting an already absent template succeeds without exposing ownership information.
- [ ] Existing editor, pending controls, cancellation, error/retry, and snapshot behavior remain intact; ordinary request failures preserve the draft.
- [ ] Requests use current credentials from the shared auth client; definitive authentication loss enters existing recovery, and account changes clear training state and ignore late results.
- [ ] Actual anonymous/two-user HTTP requests demonstrate ownership isolation across the complete template aggregate and retry metadata.
- [ ] Local Supabase checks verify CRUD, ordering, snapshots, rollback, retry behavior, and durable reads after app/service recreation and renewed access to the same account.
- [ ] Device review verifies restart/update/reinstall persistence, existing native editor behavior, and visibly labeled sample workout history. Record completed checks and any outstanding review separately.
