## Problem Statement

The template editor already lets a user create and maintain complete workout templates, but its production service stores them only in memory and restores demonstration templates on reload. Users lose saved work when the app restarts and cannot recover it after an update or reinstall. Database tables alone do not connect that workflow to durable, account-private storage.

Network failures also make saving ambiguous: the database may commit even when the app never receives the response. A reliable persistence integration must preserve the draft, allow a safe retry, and prevent partially stored templates or accidental duplicate creation.

## Solution

Replace the production template operations with authenticated backend persistence while preserving the existing editor. A successful Save stores the entire template together. Reopening restores its saved exercise descriptions, order, and targets without fetching the live catalog. Saved templates remain available to the same account on the same backend after restarts, updates, and reinstall followed by email OTP access.

New accounts begin with no saved templates. Unsaved drafts remain temporary. Failures leave the draft available for correction or retry while authentication remains valid. The Workouts tab continues to demonstrate sample history, clearly labeled as sample data until session persistence arrives in #47.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I want my saved templates stored with my account, so that restarting the app does not lose them.
2. As a returning user, I want my templates loaded after valid authentication is restored, so that I can resume planning without another unnecessary OTP.
3. As a user who reinstalls the app, I want signing into the same account to restore my saved templates, so that reinstalling does not erase my plans.
4. As a user, I want app updates to preserve my templates, so that upgrading does not discard training data.
5. As a new user, I want an empty template list with Create available, so that my account contains only templates I choose to save.
6. As a user, I want to create a complete template through the existing editor, so that persistence does not require a different workflow.
7. As a user, I want my template title and optional description preserved, so that I recognize my saved plan.
8. As a user, I want separate templates to allow the same title, so that naming does not restrict my plans.
9. As a user, I want new templates appended in a stable list order, so that reopening the app does not reshuffle them.
10. As a user, I want editing a template to keep its list position, so that updates do not unexpectedly move it.
11. As a user, I want my exercises reopened in their saved order, so that my planned sequence remains clear.
12. As a user, I want repeated placements of a catalog exercise to stay independent, so that I can give them different targets.
13. As a user, I want reordering to preserve each placement and its targets, so that moving an exercise does not exchange its sets with another placement.
14. As a user, I want saved exercise names, muscles, equipment, and available supplementary details preserved, so that catalog changes do not rewrite my plan.
15. As a user, I want saved exercise detail to open without a live catalog request, so that catalog availability does not control access to my saved description.
16. As a user, I want each placement's sets and repetition targets preserved, so that reopening restores what I planned.
17. As a user, I want zero and decimal pound targets preserved, so that valid fixed-weight targets round-trip accurately.
18. As a user, I want invalid targets and incomplete templates rejected with useful feedback, so that I can correct them before saving.
19. As a user, I want Save to commit my whole template together, so that a failure cannot leave only some exercises or targets saved.
20. As a user, I want saved list counts refreshed after a change, so that summaries match the saved template.
21. As a user, I want failed saves to retain my complete draft, so that I can retry without entering it again.
22. As a user, I want retrying a save whose response was lost to recover the same saved template, so that I do not accidentally create duplicates.
23. As a user, I want to edit a retained draft after a failed response, so that I can correct or improve it before saving again.
24. As a user, I want that edited retry to use the same template identity, so that uncertainty about an earlier creation does not create another template.
25. As a user, I want a delayed retry of an earlier save to leave a later save intact, so that retrying does not silently reverse newer changes.
26. As a user editing from two devices, I want the last committed whole-template save to become the saved version, so that the concurrency rule is predictable.
27. As a user, I want an update to a deleted template to report that it is missing, so that saving an old draft cannot resurrect it.
28. As a user, I want Cancel and discard controls to retain their existing behavior, so that unsaved changes do not become persistent accidentally.
29. As a user, I want tab changes to retain my draft during valid access, so that navigation does not lose unfinished edits.
30. As a user, I want pending writes to block conflicting actions, so that repeated taps do not submit overlapping changes.
31. As a user, I want confirmed deletion to remove the template and its children together, so that no part of the deleted plan remains visible.
32. As a user, I want retrying deletion after a lost response to succeed when the template is already gone, so that I can recover without a misleading error.
33. As a user, I want a failed deletion to retain the visible detail and retry path, so that I can recover from connection problems.
34. As a user, I want loading failures distinguished from an empty account, so that a temporary outage does not appear to erase my templates.
35. As a user, I want other accounts and anonymous requests unable to read my templates, so that my training plans remain private.
36. As a user, I want other accounts unable to change, delete, or attach records to my templates, so that ownership protects the complete plan.
37. As a user, I want ordinary connection or permission failures to preserve my draft, so that a request error does not unnecessarily sign me out.
38. As a user, I want valid token refresh to preserve my open editor, so that routine authentication maintenance does not interrupt planning.
39. As a user whose authentication has definitively ended, I want existing access recovery to clear protected state, so that stale account data is not left accessible.
40. As a user changing accounts, I want the previous account's drafts and delayed request results discarded, so that accounts cannot leak data into each other's screens.
41. As a user, I want template edits and deletion to leave workout history independent, so that planning changes cannot rewrite past performance.
42. As a user viewing Workouts before session persistence is available, I want demonstration history explicitly labeled as sample data, so that I do not confuse it with my own saved activity.

## Implementation Decisions

- Preserve MVVM and the injected asynchronous workout-service contract. Use the account-scoped service factory introduced by #118 as the production composition seam; retain controlled in-memory services for tests. Template operations use persistence, while session reads continue to return clearly labeled sample history. Do not silently fall back to sample templates when configuration or requests fail.
- Share one lazily configured Supabase client/runtime between authentication and template persistence. The factory's Account argument establishes service lifetime, not authorization. Obtain current credentials for each request; do not capture an access token when constructing the service. Preserve #118's same-account refresh behavior and account-generation cleanup.
- Keep the design's service → authenticated HTTP handler/Edge Function → data access → database boundaries. HTTP handlers validate the request and authentication, data access maps the aggregate, and a narrow transactional database function performs atomic writes with invoker rights under the requesting user's authenticated context. Never use privileged service credentials for routine template operations. Add this function and any necessary retry metadata through new migrations rather than editing #102's shared migrations. Existing ownership constraints, grants, and RLS remain authoritative; new function access and metadata must be explicitly owner-scoped.
- Provide typed request/response and service contracts for list, detail, creation, whole-template update, and deletion. Validate untrusted JSON at runtime, including nested snapshots and numbers; TypeScript types alone are insufficient. Keep the existing metadata-update method coherent with whole-template persistence rather than bypassing validation. Return canonical saved aggregates after mutations, with useful categories for validation, authentication, missing records, and retryable request failure; do not expose backend internals or another owner's existence.
- Saved templates and placements use UUIDs. Translate temporary draft placement identities when creating records, including newly added placements on an existing template. Preserve surviving placement UUIDs through edits/reordering, independent of catalog identity. Reject duplicate, foreign, or unrelated saved placement identities rather than reparenting them. Server operations determine ownership from authenticated context, never a trusted client-supplied owner.
- Store immutable creation timestamps and list templates in ascending creation-time order with UUID as a deterministic tie-breaker. New templates append under normal creation order; editing does not change creation time or list position. Read placements and sets in explicit one-based order. Ensure backend row limits cannot silently truncate a list or aggregate; the service's complete-list contract does not require a new paginated UI.
- Preserve complete descriptive snapshots from the shared catalog model: name, distinct primary and secondary muscles, equipment, and available image, instruction, and translation content. Preserve catalog identity relationally and maintain existing distinctions for missing optional data. Do not join to or fetch the live catalog when opening saved detail. Persisting image references preserves the existing loading/unavailable behavior; this feature does not download or guarantee external image availability.
- Keep template-exercise positions separate from UUID identities. Template sets retain their one-based set numbers, positive integer reps, and finite nonnegative fixed target weights in pounds, including zero and decimals. Preserve existing trimmed nonblank title and description behavior; duplicate titles are valid. Save requires at least one exercise, at least one valid set per placement, and consecutive final ordering. Incomplete drafts remain permitted before Save.
- Validate the complete aggregate and commit all metadata, membership, snapshots, ordering, and sets together. Defer ordering uniqueness within the transaction when necessary, validating the final state before commit. Failure rolls back both aggregate changes and any successful-save retry record. Deletion uses existing cascades. Database row policies are not a substitute for the whole-template rules at the save boundary.
- Assign a stable template UUID to a creation draft's persistence operation and retain its temporary-to-saved identity mapping across retries while the draft/account lifetime remains active. Associate each distinct save attempt with an owner-scoped operation identity and its content. The same operation and unchanged content recover the original committed result rather than writing again. Reject reuse of an operation identity for different content. Changing the retained draft creates a new operation against that same template identity, whether or not the earlier response arrived. Do not deduplicate by title or catalog content.
- Make successful-save recognition durable on the server and atomic with the save. Replays must not overwrite later distinct saves, reinsert deleted templates, reveal foreign records, or cross account boundaries. Check current ownership/existence before returning a historical result after deletion. A definitive failed transaction does not count as a committed operation and remains retryable. Client retry information is temporary; persisting unfinished drafts across restart is out of scope. The schema and storage representation of retry recognition are implementation choices subject to these observable guarantees.
- Serialize concurrent writes to the same template so each distinct save is a whole-template transaction. The last committed distinct save wins. Do not add version-conflict UI, merging, or live cross-device synchronization. Replaying an already committed operation is not a new save. Distinguish retrying an uncertain creation from an update: updates cannot create records, and an absent committed creation cannot be resurrected by replay.
- Owner-scoped missing/inaccessible detail reads return the existing missing-template state. Missing/inaccessible updates return the same non-disclosing missing-record failure. Deleting a valid but absent or inaccessible ID is a successful no-op; deleting a foreign ID never changes that owner's data. Invalid identifiers remain validation errors. This intentionally supersedes the in-memory service's missing-delete error behavior for the persistent contract.
- Preserve existing loading/retry, Save/Cancel, discard guards, tab-retained drafts, pending locks, saved-detail navigation, and summary refreshes. On ordinary failed writes, keep the whole draft editable and retryable. Treat a committed mutation followed by a failed refresh as a read failure, without falsely reporting that the saved transaction rolled back. The lost-response rules cover transport failures whose commit result is unknown.
- Add a narrow notification bridge from definitive protected-request authentication rejection to #118's existing account recovery. Refreshable expiry uses the shared auth runtime; a generic 403, validation failure, unavailable account record, or transport error is not evidence that authentication ended. Routine refresh preserves services/drafts; definitive auth loss, sign-out, or account change clears account-owned state and ignores late results. Do not automatically replay a previous account's pending write under a newly signed-in account.
- Do not seed or migrate the former in-memory sample templates into accounts. Keep session-history fixtures independent of persistent template identities and label them visibly as sample history. This label is the only necessary change to the Workouts experience before #47.

## Testing Decisions

- The maintainer approved two complementary existing integration boundaries: router-level behavior tests and the real production service through HTTP/Edge Function to disposable local Supabase. Prefer these high boundaries to new hook-by-hook or SQL-implementation tests. A good test asserts visible behavior or saved outcomes, not component layout structure, incidental SDK call sequences, SQL text, helper names, or policy names.
- Reuse the existing root injection/account-scoped factory, real Views/ViewModels/navigation, and controlled service wrappers for loading, pending, validation, failure, retry, cancellation, and account-lifecycle scenarios. Existing template builder/editor/navigation and auth-navigation suites provide prior art. Keep focused service-contract checks only where they expose distinct identity/snapshot outcomes efficiently.
- Run actual production template service requests through the local endpoint and database using nonprivileged authenticated clients. Provision two test accounts and application Users administratively only for setup, following the existing disposable authentication-check approach. Permission assertions must use anonymous or the relevant user's credentials, never an administrative bypass.
- Round-trip creation, read/list, whole-template edits, addition/removal, reordering, deletion, duplicate titles, stable list order, UUID stability, zero/decimal weights, independent repeated placements, and all optional snapshot content. Saved detail must not request catalog JSON. Cover empty accounts, missing records, invalid payloads, and complete results when backend row limits would otherwise truncate them.
- Prove rollback with a failure during a multirow write after some work has begun, not only a payload rejected before writing. Confirm the previously saved aggregate and successful-operation recognition remain unchanged. Verify two actual saves cannot interleave into a mixed aggregate.
- Simulate a committed save whose response is lost, then retry unchanged content and confirm one template and the original result. Edit the retained draft and save again to the same template identity; replay the earlier operation and confirm it cannot undo the later state. Reject the same operation identity with changed content. Cover independent devices' last-committed-save rule, delete-response loss, update-after-delete, and creation replay after deletion without resurrection.
- Verify actual anonymous and cross-user list/detail/mutation requests, guessed template/placement IDs, foreign-parent attachment, and operation-identity reuse cannot disclose or change another user's aggregate or replay data. Include successful owner operations so a deny-everything implementation cannot pass. Reuse #102's database suite for its existing row-policy/constraint/cascade coverage; add targeted database checks for new functions or retry metadata as needed.
- Verify ordinary failed writes preserve the draft, read failures do not appear as empty data, pending controls prevent duplicate taps, and missing/idempotent-delete outcomes match the contract. Verify a committed save plus failed subsequent read offers read recovery rather than an incorrect rollback claim.
- Verify token refresh keeps the editor/draft intact, definitive request auth loss enters recovery, connection/permission failures do not spuriously sign out, and account changes/sign-out discard old drafts and late responses. Reuse #118's lifecycle tests rather than reimplementing its restoration behavior.
- Recreate the app/service with the same backend and account, restore authentication or sign in again, and assert saved templates remain. Temporary drafts need not survive. Separately perform supported-device review for app restart/update and reinstall followed by OTP access to the same account; automated service recreation alone does not establish every native lifecycle claim.
- Verify the Workouts tab labels sample history clearly and template edits/deletion leave its independent data unchanged. Retain existing native drag/accessibility, themes, keyboard, and increased-text-size review where persistence integration affects them.
- During implementation run the checked-in TypeScript/Jest checks, database checks for additive migrations, and a documented repeatable local full-stack template check. Extend the disposable verification approach to serve required Edge Functions without resetting or modifying a shared/hosted backend. Run relevant Expo/native checks for changed app composition. Record which checks actually ran and which require reviewer/device follow-up.

## Out of Scope

- Rebuilding #102's foundation tables, replacing its ownership policies, rewriting shared migration history, or expanding into a general persistence framework. New transactional functions and private retry metadata needed by #45 are included.
- Reimplementing OTP, auth restoration, sign-out, or account switching. Only shared-client composition and the protected-request recovery bridge are included; #43's lifecycle contract remains authoritative.
- Workout-session logging or persistence, session recovery, personal exercise maximums, percentage targets, or unit conversion. These remain #47 and #37/#49 and related M2 work.
- Offline reads/writes, background save queues, persisted unsaved drafts, cross-device live refresh, conflict detection/merging, and automatic refresh of saved snapshots from catalog changes.
- Catalog caching/retry changes, external-image caching, template duplication, exercise swapping, or other editor redesigns.
- Automatic sample/user seeding, importing lost prior in-memory templates, automatic hosted deployment, account-deletion UI, or marking the feature complete merely because the specification is published.

## Further Notes

- Canonical terms come from the root glossary. Template drafts are unsaved changes; template exercises are independent placements with saved catalog descriptions; workout history is separate from templates. No new domain term needs a glossary entry. Existing snapshot and independent-history ADRs remain authoritative. A new ADR records the transactional save boundary and requesting-user execution context.

## Final review corrections

An additive validation migration aligns direct save RPC nonblank text with the
shared wire model, including Unicode whitespace. Authenticated RPC checks reject
blank main, start, peak, and optional image references, along with unusable names,
equipment, translations, and catalog identities. Rejected writes leave no saved
aggregate, and corrected content can reuse the same operation identity, proving
that no successful-save receipt was committed. The real HTTP regression for an
out-of-range repetition count now returns validation/400 rather than unavailable/503.
Both issues were reproduced before correction; the complete fresh-backend check,
TypeScript/Jest, and clean/populated database checks were rerun for these changes.

The PR-comment review also reproduced a stale mutation retry after recovery into
a new session for the same account. Production services now check both account
identity and the captured generation before dispatch, after session lookup, and
before renewal/retry. Public-service and router regressions cover discarded
requests after re-entry to either the same or a different account; the old request
is not resent and cannot end the newly loaded account's access.

The editor and shared HTTP contract now reject repetition targets above the
existing integer storage maximum with correction feedback. Additive migration
`00600` enforces that same bound for direct RPC callers; the full-stack check
rejects an out-of-range write without consuming its operation identity, then
saves the inclusive maximum. This review migration is pending the next reviewed
hosted rollout; the earlier device report covers the deployment through `00500`.

The populated migration check also reproduces the parallel review order (`00400`
before missing `00300`). It first failed with `MigrationMissingRemoteError`;
documented `db push --include-all` now applies the missing migration while
preserving saved templates. Already-deployed migration versions remain unchanged.
After these review corrections, all 139 Jest tests, TypeScript, the three fresh
HTTP suites, 100 database assertions, and iOS/Android exports passed.

## Hosted rollout and physical-device verification

On November 18, 2026, the maintainer reported that even a minimal template failed
to save during hosted physical-device review. The configured template endpoint
returned 404 because it had not been deployed; hosted migration history contained
only the two foundation migrations. The deployment dry run identified the five
pending template migrations.

With explicit maintainer authorization, all five migrations were applied to the
shared OpenFit development project and `workout-templates` was deployed. Migration
history then matched the checkout, the function was active at version 1, and an
unauthenticated request returned the handler's expected authentication/401 response
instead of 404.

After deployment, the maintainer reported: “Hosted verification on a physical
device passes.” This is maintainer-reported device evidence; the report did not
enumerate individual platforms or each scenario in the audit checklist. The agent
did not independently operate the physical device.

## Review still required

The PR-comment Codex review loop, independent non-author contributor approval,
maintainer merge, and the repository's post-merge author/non-author production
audit remain separate completion requirements. See [setup](setup.md) for
repeatable isolated checks and the [maintainer rollout checklist](maintainers.md#template-rollout-audit)
for deployment ordering and the individual device/hosted audit scenarios.
### Exercise catalog boundary (#44)

RepDB JSON is validated at the service boundary into a shared catalog exercise
model with a namespaced catalog identifier, English name, separate primary and
secondary muscles, and explicit equipment requirements. Optional images,
instructions, and German/Spanish content are retained in the model.
Usable records are returned with diagnostics for malformed data; an unusable
response has a distinct failure result.

The #83 implementation adds a temporary standalone catalog screen opened from
Templates. A separately injected catalog service receives an HTTP request
function and loads the single JSON document at
`https://exercise-dataset.com/exercises.json`, using the existing mapper. The
ViewModel exposes loading, usable results, and defined transport/response failure
states. A virtualized list shows exercises alphabetically with colloquial muscle
groups and equipment. Primary and secondary groups remain separate; raw muscles
remain unchanged in the model. Rejected records produce a quiet partial-results
notice; optional-content diagnostics alone do not. Each visit loads afresh,
retaining results while open, with Back available on failure. Caching, retries,
and adding or saving exercises in the template editor remain separate work.
The #84 implementation combines case-insensitive exercise-name search with one
primary muscle-group filter, defaulting to All muscles. Secondary targets never
cause filter matches. No-match results offer Clear search and filter without

Project communication with take place on GitHub Discussions. It will be used for the main communication functions:

- Announcements
- PR review requests
- Issue assignment requests
- All other project communication

Response times for development dependent tasks such as issue assignment and review requests will be responded to **within 48 hours**. That's our commitment.

Project-wide decisions are made by the project maintainers, with input from the entire project community. Issue #136 proposes replacing Supabase and email sign-in with on-device SQLite and first-launch name entry. Templates, workout history, and personal exercise maximums would live on the device. That would let users save workouts offline and remove the backend for personal data, at the cost of cross-device sync and the current ability to recover templates by signing in after a reinstall. The issue is open and has no comments. [GitHub issue #136](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/136)

The hosted template flow has been verified on a physical device, so the cutover needs an explicit decision about existing data. The app already uses injected services, and saved templates carry their own exercise details. Those boundaries give us a way to change storage while preserving the editor and keeping saved workouts independent of the live catalog. [Hosted verification](/Users/james/.t3/worktrees/open-fit/t3-f7fb88c6-c306a9bb3b4ca272/docs/issue-125-template-production.md:84) · [Service architecture](/Users/james/.t3/worktrees/open-fit/t3-f7fb88c6-c306a9bb3b4ca272/docs/adr/0002-use-mvvm-with-injected-services.md) · [Catalog snapshots](/Users/james/.t3/worktrees/open-fit/t3-f7fb88c6-c306a9bb3b4ca272/docs/adr/issue-44-catalog-identity-and-snapshots.md)

## Round 1

❓ **Q1 — Is one device the product model?** If someone logs a workout on their phone and opens the app on a tablet that evening, are you comfortable with each device having its own workout history? Is that a deliberate product choice or a concession to ship the MVP?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Make a single device the supported MVP model. Revisit sync if users demonstrate a need to train across devices.

---

❓ **Q2 — What do we owe people with Supabase templates?** If the hosted project contains templates someone relies on, should retiring it require a verified way for that person to keep them? What evidence would make you comfortable skipping migration?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Check what the hosted environment contains before deciding. If anyone relies on their templates, make a verified transfer path a condition of retirement. If the records are all disposable test data, skip migration.

---

❓ **Q3 — Is recovery part of the local-storage promise?** A user logs six months of workouts and loses their phone. Should the first release that stores real workout history already provide a way to back it up and restore it, or is that an acceptable limitation for the MVP?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Require manual export and import before people are expected to rely on the app as their workout history. An internal demo can ship earlier. Moving existing Supabase templates is a separate decision from protecting future on-device records.

---

❓ **Q4 — What must work on the first launch in airplane mode?** Should a fresh install be able to create a template from the exercise catalog, or is the offline promise limited to using templates already saved on the device?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Make text-based exercise selection, template editing, workout logging, and history work offline. Allow illustrations to load when connected. Confirm that the catalog license permits bundling before committing to RepDB as the offline source. [Current catalog design](/Users/james/.t3/worktrees/open-fit/t3-f7fb88c6-c306a9bb3b4ca272/docs/design.md:145)

---

❓ **Q5 — What earns the name prompt its place?** What should the name do for the user on a single-device app? If they leave it blank, is there a reason to keep them from opening the app?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Make the name optional. If it only personalizes a greeting, open the app directly and let users add it later.

---

❓ **Q6 — Does SQLite become the foundation for M2?** Should the project settle #136 before building persistence for workout history and personal exercise maximums, or does the milestone need to ship on the current backend first?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Decide #136 before implementing the storage work in #47 and #49. If you choose SQLite, build those features on it and keep #48 focused on the workout flow through the existing service boundary. That avoids building two new persistence paths that the proposal would immediately replace. [Session persistence #47](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/47) · [Workout screens #48](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/48) · [Exercise maximums #49](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/49)

Single-device use is the MVP model. The Supabase records are disposable test data, so the cutover needs no migration. Backup and recovery go on the roadmap. First launch requires a name, and we’ll settle #136 before continuing the M2 persistence work.

## Round 2

❓ **Q7 — What works at the gym with zero signal?** My recommendation is that a fresh install can complete onboarding, search and filter exercises, read instructions, build a template, log a workout, and review history in airplane mode. Bundle a pinned version of RepDB’s catalog data and load illustrations when connected. RepDB documents local JSON bundles for Expo and permits attributed in-app use. Is text-only exercise detail enough offline, or are illustrations essential at the gym? [RepDB Expo example](https://repdb.co/examples/react-native/) · [RepDB Free Tier license](https://github.com/RepDB/exercise-dataset/blob/main/LICENSE-DATA.md)

---

❓ **Q8 — Where does the personalization show up?** The name is required because you want the app to feel personal. Where should the user see that benefit after setup?

➡️ **My recommendation** is to greet the user by name on the Templates screen they land on, and let them edit their display name in Settings. Keep the same workout data when the name changes.

---

❓ **Q9 — What survives an interrupted workout?** #48 already calls for preserving the active session through locking and reopening the phone. Suppose the OS kills the app after the user records four sets. Should reopening restore those sets and offer to resume? [Workout logging and history #48](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/48)

➡️ **My recommendation** is to persist one active session as the user logs each set and offer to resume it after a restart. Add it to workout history when they finish or stop it.

---

❓ **Q10 — When should users learn the limits of recovery?** With backups deferred, when should we tell users that app removal or loss of the phone can mean loss of their workout data?

➡️ **My recommendation** is one short line on the name screen, with the same information available later in Settings. For example, “Your workouts are saved on this device. You may lose them if you delete the app or lose your phone.”

---

❓ **Q11 — What proves SQLite is ready for M2?** What should work before #47 and #49 begin relying on the new storage layer?

➡️ **My recommendation** is to prove the existing template flow first. On a supported device in airplane mode, enter a name, create a template from the bundled catalog, force-close the app, then reopen, edit, and delete the template. Use that verified SQLite foundation for workout sessions and personal exercise maximums.

**Saving each logged set should feel immediate.** The write is small and local. Update the screen right away, then use Expo SQLite’s async API to save the changed set in the background. The workout timer can run from the saved start time without writing on every tick. If a write fails, keep the entered values visible and offer Retry. We should verify rapid set logging and force-close recovery on a physical device before calling the behavior ready. [Expo SQLite](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/sdk/sqlite/) · [SQLite write-ahead logging](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)

We’ve agreed that illustrations are essential at the gym, the Templates screen greets the user by name, interrupted workouts can be resumed, name entry includes a small local-storage and backup notice, and template workflow parity is the gate for moving on to M2.

## Round 3

❓ **Q12 — Should all exercise illustrations ship with the app?** RepDB’s flat illustrations total **20.3 MB in the source package**. The impact on the final app download still needs to be measured. Bundling them would let someone open any exercise detail in airplane mode immediately after installing. [Published RepDB package](https://registry.npmjs.org/@repdb/exercises/-/exercises-2026.11.1.tgz) · [RepDB Expo example](https://repdb.co/examples/react-native/)

➡️ **My recommendation** is to bundle all flat illustrations, including both poses where available. Is that an acceptable size trade-off for first-launch offline use?

---

❓ **Q13 — What counts as logged?** A user types a weight and rep count, then the app closes before they mark the set complete. Should those in-progress values come back too?

➡️ **My recommendation** is to save when the user marks a set complete or confirms an edit to a logged set. On resume, restore every successfully saved set. That gives users a clear point at which a set becomes part of the record.

---

❓ **Q14 — What should Resume open?** If a workout is still active when the user reopens the app, should we take them straight back into it, or let them decide what to do from the Templates screen?

➡️ **My recommendation** is to show a prominent **Resume workout** action on Templates. Keep one active workout at a time. If they try to start another, offer to resume or stop the current workout first.

name: to-spec
description: "Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker: no interview, just synthesis of what you've already discussed."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

This skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec. Do NOT interview the user; just synthesize what you already know.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven't already. Use the project's domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you're touching.

2. Sketch out the seams at which you're going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.

Check with the user that these seams match their expectations.

3. Write the spec using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.

<spec-template>

## Problem Statement

The problem that the user is facing, from the user's perspective.

## Solution

The solution to the problem, from the user's perspective.

## User Stories

A LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:

1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>

<user-story-example>
1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending
</user-story-example>

This list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.

## Implementation Decisions

A list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:

- The modules that will be built/modified
- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified
- Technical clarifications from the developer
- Architectural decisions
- Schema changes
- API contracts
- Specific interactions

Do NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.

Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.

## Testing Decisions

A list of testing decisions that were made. Include:

- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)
- Which modules will be tested
- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)

## Out of Scope

A description of the things that are out of scope for this spec.

## Further Notes

Any further notes about the feature.

</spec-template>

name: grilling
description: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
---

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

# Contributing to LibreLift

This project welcomes the time and efforts of the community.

## First Steps

To get started do these four things:

- Fork the repo and walk through the [setup guide](./docs/setup.md) to get the app running on your local machine. Ensure that you have a mobile device to test app builds on, or can access iOS/Android simulators.

- Review the [communication standards](./docs/communication-standards.md). This outlines where project communication happens and when to expect responses. 

- Review the [git standards](./docs/git-standards.md) before working. This outlines the process we have established to keep the project organized and maintainable. All contributors and maintainers are expected to follow them.

- Review the [project management guide](./docs/project-mgmt.md) to learn how to use the project board, choose work, and follow the triage and milestone process.

## Developing

Once you are able to setup and run the project locally, you are ready to start developing. To get started, look for issues marked with the "good first issue" label. These will give you a chance to get acquainted with our development standards and project architecture. For experienced contributors or maintainers, focus efforts on issues with no one else assigned, or those marked "help wanted".

After picking an issue, request a maintainer to assign you to an issue using the method outlined in those standard. If needed, check the [communication standards](./docs/communication-standards.md) to see how to do this.

If you plan on using AI, make sure to review [AI Guidelines] (to be added soon)

## PR Process

To keep PRs a manageable size for humans and agents, there is a cap of one logical change or roughly 1000 lines, whichever comes first. The 1,000 lines is a soft limit as some pull requests will include things like `package-lock.json` that don't need to be heavily reviewed. 

If a single logical change/feature extends beyond 1k lines, split it into multiple PRs or a [stacked PR](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/stacked-pull-requests). This will make the review process and the PR history cleaner and more manageable.

## Review Process

When a PR is ready for review, request someone who did not author the PR to review it, either through GitHub of the communication channel.

Having someone who didn't write the code review it will help with the quality of the project. A fresh set of eyes ensures that we aren't making incorrect assumptions or poor design choices.

Usually there will be some discussion about your changes and a few iterations of revision, review, and revision again to find the solution that works best.

After approval from an independent reviewer the PR will be merged into `main`.

# Git standards

How a change gets into this project. If you're contributing, this is how
we work; if you think a rule is wrong, open an issue and say why.

## Branch names

**The rule**: `type/issue#-two-words`. 

**Example**: `feat/31-integrated-timer`.

**The reason**: This allows branches to be easily categorized, and connects them directly to open issues. At any given moment we can know what work is being done on any issue by seeing the open branches for that issue.

## Commit messages

**The rule**: Follow [cbeam's 7 rules](https://cbea.ms/git-commit/) for useful commit messages, and prefix all commits with [conventional commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary) types.

**Example**:

```
fix: correct expected json payload for getTemplates endpoint

The getTemplates endpoint was expecting a single JSON object 
and was trying to serialize it into a WorkoutTemplate object.

The endpoint from the backend actually returns a list of 
JSON objects, so the frontend client was changed to 
expect that instead.
```

**The reason**: Similar to the branch names prefixes, conventional commit prefixes allow commits to be easily categorized. The type of work being done in a PR can be easily viewed from commit messages. Also, this format supports one-line summaries such as in GitHub, but provide more info when necessary. 

## Pull requests

**The rule**: Changes that resolve one issue, or 1,000 lines, whichever comes first. If an issue's resolution requires more than 1,000 lines of code, it should be decomposed.

**The reason**: PRs should be easily human reviewable, so they should be kept small and manageable in size.

## Review

**The rule**: At one approval from a contributor who did not author the PR

**The reason**: Having a fresh set of eyes can help expose untested assumptions. Also, having to explain a PR to someone independent of its development proves understanding.

## Merging

**The rule**: Only maintainers have permission to merge. The merging method that will be used is squash and merge.

**The reason**: Protecting the `main` branch by limiting merge permissions will keep the production code safe. Squash and merge will keep the history clean and linear, and allow entire features to be rolled back with one command if necessary.

## Definition of done

**The rule**: A PR is merged to `main` after adequate review and passing tests locally and in CI. Use `npm run test` from the repo root for local tests. A CI pipeline has not been configured yet. Additionally, the PR must then be audited in the production environment to ensure functionality.

To get a PR merged you must also implement necessary documentation updates, either as part of the PR or by filing the issue(s) for the documentation changes needed and including the issue link in the PR description. If the documentation change is made separately, it must be be completed and have a PR created before the feature PR will be merged.

**Definitions:** 
- "adequate review" means that the "Review" rule above have been applied: one non-author contributor has reviewed the PR and given it their approval. 
- "Necessary documentation changes" includes, but is not limited to: updating the [design doc](./design.md) if actual implementation differs from documented design or design decisions that are made, adding or editing a component description, or adding/editing code comments. Documentation changes (excluding code comments) will be reviewed and approved by a maintainer.
- "audited in the production environment" means that the PR author and a non-author contributor (can be the same one who reviewed the PR, or a different one) will verify that all of the acceptance criteria for the feature listed in the connected issue are satisfied in the production environment. The results of this audit is recorded in the merged PR's comments. That way if the PR needs to be reverted and re-opened, the PR history and audit results are all in one place.

**The reason**: A task is not truly "done" until we can verify that it passes tests and works in production. And, documentation updates are part of being "done" because they are part of the development process, not a separate, administrative task.
# Triage roles: existing labels and board status

The skills' canonical roles map to combinations of existing labels, project
Status, issue state, and the implementation brief. This adapter replaces the
skills' default one-label-per-role convention; it creates no new labels or fields.

## Categories

- `bug`: a failure in existing behavior.
- `enhancement`: an improvement or new behavior.
- `documentation` and `accessibility` describe relevant subject matter; they do
  not substitute for a bug/enhancement classification during triage.

The bug-report template currently defaults to `documentation, needs triage`.
For an app bug, apply `bug` and retain `documentation` only if the report also
concerns documentation.

## State roles

| Canonical role | Existing labels | Project Status / issue state | Brief field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `needs-triage` | `needs triage` | Backlog; open | Maintainer evaluation pending |
| `needs-info` | `question` | Backlog; open | Identify the missing reporter information |
| `ready-for-agent` | `planned work` | Ready; open; prerequisites satisfied | `Implementation: agent` |
| `ready-for-human` | `planned work` | Ready; open; prerequisites satisfied | `Implementation: human`, with the reason |
| `wontfix` | `non-goal` for a scope rejection | Closed as `not planned` | Record why the request is declined |

`planned work` alone means accepted scope, not readiness or permission to start.
Agent-ready and human-ready work share existing labels and Status; distinguish
them in the brief rather than inferring an executor from `help wanted` or an assignee.
If the brief does not name an executor, resolve that before treating it as either
ready role. Remove the previous triage-state label when moving to a different role.

Use the existing execution statuses after work begins: In progress, In review,
and Done. Done follows the repository's definition of done; it is not a synonym
for any closed issue. Keep rejected requests out of Done; archive their Backlog
board items when removal from active views is authorized.

## Waiting and closure distinctions

- The live `question` description requests information from the issue author;
  use it for `needs-info`.
- The live `awaiting response` description means the issue author is waiting for
  a maintainer reply. Preserve it for that direction of communication; it is not
  an alias for `needs-info`.
- A duplicate uses `duplicate` and links the original issue. An already-delivered
  request points to the implementation. Neither automatically becomes `non-goal`.
- Deferred work stays in Backlog with its disposition explained; deferral alone
  is not a rejection.
- Preserve unrelated labels such as `epic` and `good first issue`.

If labels, the implementation brief, and board Status conflict, report the conflict
and ask the maintainer to resolve it before advancing the issue. Existing label
descriptions and the board's field names were checked on November 9, 2026.
# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs live in [LibreLift/libre-lift](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues).
Use the `gh` CLI with `--repo LibreLift/libre-lift` for issue operations. The local
origin still uses the former `LibreLift/expo_suite` name, which GitHub redirects.

Read [project management](../project-mgmt.md) before tracker changes. Use its
issue templates, milestone rules, assignment process, and definition of done.

## Issue operations

- Read: `gh issue view NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --comments`.
- List: `gh issue list --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --state open --json number,title,labels,assignees`.
- Create: `gh issue create --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --title TITLE --body-file FILE --label LABEL`.
- Comment: `gh issue comment NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --body-file FILE`.
- Labels: `gh issue edit NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --add-label LABEL --remove-label LABEL`.
- Close: `gh issue close NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --reason REASON`;
  use `completed` for delivered work or `not planned` for declined/superseded work.

Write multiline bodies to a file and pass `--body-file`. Use the matching
`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` structure. During triage, every published issue or comment
must start with `> *This was generated by AI during triage.*`.

## Project board

The board is [LibreLift MVP, organization project 1](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1).
Issue labels and board fields are separate. Use the mapping in
[triage labels](./triage-labels.md) for readiness and execution roles.

Inspect current fields with `gh project field-list 1 --owner LibreLift --format json`
and items with `gh project item-list 1 --owner LibreLift --format json`. Resolve
current project, field, item, and option IDs before a board edit; use
`gh project item-edit` for field changes. Check view filters before treating an
item as absent. Reuse the existing Status and Task Size fields and their options.

Project reads require the `read:project` token scope; writes require `project`.
If CLI access is unavailable, the public board can be inspected read-only. Report
blocked board edits and leave them pending rather than claiming synchronization.

## Dependencies and claiming work

Use native GitHub sub-issues for epics and native issue dependencies for blockers.
If unavailable, record `Part of #NUMBER` and `Blocked by: #NUMBER` links in the
issue body. A blocked task is not Ready. Apply `planned work` only with maintainer
authorization; follow the repository's assignment process before claiming work.

When a skill says to publish a spec or fetch a ticket, create or read a GitHub
issue in this repository. Follow repository label mappings instead of creating
labels named after a skill or its internal roles.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.**

# Setup

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 24 (`.nvmrc`) and npm. With nvm, run `nvm install` and `nvm use`.
- Expo Go supporting SDK 58 on an iPhone or Android device.
- A computer and phone on the same Wi-Fi network; internet for email access and
  the live exercise catalog.

`package.json` selects Expo SDK 58; `package-lock.json` pins installed versions.
The version in `app.json` is the app release, not the SDK. Use committed versions.
For SDK upgrades, follow [Expo's guide](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/upgrading-expo-sdk-walkthrough/),
then run `npx expo install --fix` and `npx expo-doctor`.

Supabase settings are required to sign in and reach training screens; without
settings, the app opens account access and appearance Settings only. Templates
and account names persist in Supabase. Workout history remains clearly labeled
sample data until session persistence is available. The template endpoint and
committed migrations must be deployed before using the new app.
Docker and Supabase CLI are optional for hosted development.

## Install and launch

```sh
git clone https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift.git
cd libre-lift
npm ci
cp .env.example .env
```

Configure `.env` using **Backend setup** below, then run `npm start`.
This runs `expo start --go` on port 8081 by default; keep the terminal running.

1. Install the matching Expo Go build; sign into Expo Go and the CLI if prompted
   (`npx expo login`). Android builds are at [Expo Go downloads](https://expo.dev/go).
2. Join the computer's Wi-Fi network. On iPhone, scan the terminal QR code with
   Camera and open in Expo Go; on Android, scan from Expo Go.
3. Allow local network access if prompted. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

For configured simulators/emulators, use `npm run ios` (Xcode) or
`npm run android` (Android Studio).
If LAN access fails, check permissions, VPN, firewall, and Wi-Fi device isolation.
Alternatively, install `npm install --global @expo/ngrok` and run
`npm start -- --tunnel`; tunneling requires internet. Restart Expo after `.env` edits.

## Checks

```sh
npm run typecheck
npm test
npx expo-doctor
npx expo export --platform ios --platform android --output-dir dist
```

These check types, Jest behavior, Expo dependencies, and native JavaScript bundles.
Jest needs no backend or credentials. Bundling does not replace device review.
No CI workflow, lint, or format script is checked in. Backend checks are below.

## Device review

- Sign in by email code, complete name onboarding, and edit the account name.
  Check invalid codes, resend, and failure recovery; training must stay gated.
- Create, edit, reorder, and delete templates. Check set targets, Save/Cancel,
  draft preservation across tabs, and discard confirmation when leaving.
- Search/filter the catalog, inspect images/instructions, and add an exercise to
  a draft. Check Back preserves browsing state and offline errors are clear.
- Open saved template exercises and expand workout history to review set details.
- Check keyboard access, increased text size, and Light/Dark/System appearance.
  Reload to confirm appearance, account names, templates, and valid account access persist.

Saved templates survive app restarts and updates. After reinstall, email OTP access
to the same account/backend restores them. Unsaved drafts remain temporary.
Workout logging and real workout-history persistence are not implemented.

## Frontend structure

- `app/`: Expo Router account access, name onboarding, Settings, and guarded tabs.
- `src/views/`: Native screens rendering ViewModel state.
- `src/viewmodels/`: Auth, theme, loading/retry, catalog, and shared template drafts.
- `src/models/`: Template, session, and exercise types with snapshot/validation rules.
- `src/services/`: Async service contracts, sample training data, Supabase Auth/User
  access, HTTP catalog mapping, and appearance storage.
- `src/theme/`: Shared light/dark colors.

The root layout injects workout, auth, catalog, and preference dependencies.
Its lazy Supabase runtime exposes the same client to authentication and feature
services, so later requests use the current authenticated session after refresh.
The injected persistence service's whole-template update and retry contract is
documented in [template updates](issue-123-template-updates.md), including its
disposable local service/HTTP/database check.
Production template operations use the authenticated persistence service; views do
not import fixtures. Controlled service factories remain available for tests. Template mutations refresh reads. Catalog requests accept injected HTTP;
results belong to the open visit, and detail shares its selected record. Adding
an exercise copies a snapshot into the draft. Catalog caching/retry are deferred.

## Backend setup

### Configure the hosted connection

In `.env` copied from `.env.example`, keep `EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` and replace
`EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` with the development project's publishable
key from a maintainer. No Supabase account/dashboard access is needed for this.
Never use database passwords or secret/service-role keys in app settings.
Git ignores `.env`. Restart Expo after changes.

### Check the backend

Open <https://jibzcwwursyzvvthazby.supabase.co/functions/v1/health>; expect
`{"status":"ok"}`. This checks function reachability only, not app credentials,
email delivery, or database access. Ask a maintainer about deployment failures.
Account access needs the application User migration and hosted Auth configuration
below. Template persistence additionally requires all committed migrations and the
`workout-templates` Edge Function; health alone does not establish that they work.

### Optional: run your own local backend

Install and start [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/).
From the repository root, use the pinned Supabase CLI 3.1.0:

```sh
npx --yes supabase@3.1.0 start
npx --yes supabase@3.1.0 status
npx --yes supabase@3.1.0 db push --include-all
npx --yes supabase@3.1.0 db query --read-only 'select 1 as connected'
```

`db push --include-all` applies pending migrations, including older-numbered
changes from parallel branches; the query should return
`connected: 1`. First startup downloads images.
Set BOTH `.env` values to the local URL and publishable key from `status`.
Use `http://127.0.0.1:54321` on the computer, `http://10.0.2.2:54321` for Android
emulators, or the computer's LAN IP for a physical phone. Restart Expo.
Studio is at <http://127.0.0.1:54323>; test emails at <http://127.0.0.1:54324>.
In another terminal, run `npx --yes supabase@3.1.0 functions serve`;
<http://127.0.0.1:54321/functions/v1/health> should return `{"status":"ok"}`.
# LibreLift

LibreLift helps individuals plan reusable workouts, record their performance,
and review their workout history. These terms distinguish planned training from
what happened during a particular session.

## Language

### People and access

**User**:
A person who plans and records their training in LibreLift and owns their workout
templates and workout sessions.

**Account**:
The identity through which a user signs in and accesses their saved training data.
_Avoid_: User when referring specifically to sign-in identity

**Account name**:
The name a user chooses to display for their account. It can be changed without
changing the email address used to sign in.
_Avoid_: Username when implying a unique sign-in identifier

### Planning

**Exercise**:
A movement, such as a bench press or squat, described by its name, target muscles,
and equipment.

**Exercise catalog**:
The collection of exercises available for inclusion in workout templates.
_Avoid_: Workout catalog, template library

**Catalog exercise**:
A named movement in the exercise catalog, with an identity shared by every template
or session that references it.
_Avoid_: Template exercise, session exercise

**Primary muscles**:
The muscles identified by the catalog as the main targets of an exercise. Missing
targets remain unspecified rather than being inferred.
_Avoid_: All target muscles

**Secondary muscles**:
The muscles identified by the catalog as supporting targets of an exercise,
distinct from its primary muscles. Missing targets remain unspecified rather than
being inferred.
_Avoid_: Primary muscles

**Muscle group**:
A broader category of muscles described by a familiar training label, such as
Chest, Upper back, Lower back, or Calves.
_Avoid_: Primary muscle when referring to the broader category

**No equipment**:
An exercise's explicit lack of required equipment, identified from the catalog's
bodyweight designation when equipment is absent. Missing equipment without that
designation is not evidence that no equipment is required.
_Avoid_: Unknown equipment

**Workout template**:
A reusable workout description containing exercises and their planned sets.
“Template” is its short name.
_Avoid_: Plan, routine (as separate domain concepts)

**Template draft**:
Unsaved changes to a workout template. These changes are separate from the saved
template until the user saves them.

**Template exercise**:
A placement of a catalog exercise within a workout template, with its own identity,
saved exercise details, and planned sets. The same catalog exercise can appear in
multiple placements; catalog changes do not change saved templates.
_Avoid_: Exercise when referring specifically to its inclusion in a template

**Template set**:
A planned set for a template exercise, with a target weight and target repetition
count.
_Avoid_: Round

### Performing and reviewing

**Workout session**:
One occurrence of performing a workout based on a workout template. “Session” is
its short name.
_Avoid_: Workout when the distinction from a workout template matters

**Session exercise**:
A placement of a catalog exercise within a workout session, with its own identity,
saved exercise details, and session sets. Its catalog identity is retained, and
catalog changes do not change saved workout history.
_Avoid_: Template exercise when referring to a session's exercise

**Session set**:
A set belonging to a session exercise, with planned targets and the performance
recorded for that session.
_Avoid_: Round, template set when referring to a session's set

**Workout history**:
The collection of saved past workout sessions available for review.
_Avoid_: Workout log, log (as names for a separate domain concept)

### Sets and performance

**Repetition**:
One performance of an exercise's movement. “Rep” is its short name.

**Set**:
A group of repetitions of one exercise; it belongs to that exercise rather than
grouping several exercises together.
_Avoid_: Round, circuit

**Target performance**:
The planned weight and repetition count for a set.
_Avoid_: Goal when referring specifically to a set's targets

**Fixed-weight target**:
A target weight expressed directly as an amount of weight.

**Personal exercise maximum**:
The weight a user records as their maximum for one repetition of a particular
exercise. It is the reference weight for percentage-based targets.

**Percentage-based target**:
A target weight expressed as a percentage of the user's personal maximum for that
exercise.

**Recorded performance**:
The weight and repetition count recorded for a session set, which may differ from
its target performance. “Actual” is a synonym for these recorded values.

# ADR Format

ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily: only when the first ADR is needed.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of the decision}

{1-3 sentences: what's the context, what did we decide, and why.}
```

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why*, not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`): useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options**: only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences**: only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it: you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library: just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it; otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.
# GLOSSARY.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.
- **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

## Single vs multi-context repos

**Single context (most repos):** One `GLOSSARY.md` at the repo root.

**Multiple contexts:** A `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` at the repo root lists the contexts, where they live, and how they relate to each other:

```md
# Glossary Map

## Contexts

- [Ordering](./src/ordering/GLOSSARY.md): receives and tracks customer orders
- [Billing](./src/billing/GLOSSARY.md): generates invoices and processes payments
- [Fulfillment](./src/fulfillment/GLOSSARY.md): manages warehouse picking and shipping

## Relationships

- **Ordering → Fulfillment**: Ordering emits `OrderPlaced` events; Fulfillment consumes them to start picking
- **Fulfillment → Billing**: Fulfillment emits `ShipmentDispatched` events; Billing consumes them to generate invoices
- **Ordering ↔ Billing**: Shared types for `CustomerId` and `Money`
```

The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `GLOSSARY.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `GLOSSARY.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.
# Domain documentation

LibreLift has one domain context, with a root glossary and shared ADR directory.

Before exploring domain code, designing a change, or naming concepts in issues,
tests, and documentation:

1. Read [GLOSSARY.md](../../GLOSSARY.md) and use its canonical terms.
2. Read the relevant records in [docs/adr/](../adr/README.md).
3. For the initial UI, read the [foundation decisions](../ui-foundation.md).

Keep the glossary limited to domain meanings. Record implementation choices in
the design documentation or an ADR when the decision has a consequential trade-off.
Surface contradictions with an existing term or ADR before changing its meaning.
Use the domain-modeling flow to resolve gaps and update documentation as decisions
are agreed. If a referenced domain document is absent, continue; create it when
there is a resolved term or decision to record.
# Share hosted development while keeping schema changes reproducible

Contributors normally run the app against the existing LibreLift hosted development
project, with an optional local Docker backend for isolated backend work. App access
uses a public key and feature-defined data permissions; hosted administration and
manual deployments remain restricted to maintainers.

Committed migrations define the database schema. Dashboard edits remain available,
but lasting schema changes must be captured in migrations and verified through a
local rebuild before being shared. This preserves dashboard flexibility while
allowing contributors to reproduce the backend without hosted administrative access.
Automated deployments are deferred to later M1 or M2.
# Use email OTP for account access

During the [#42](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues/42) design discussion
on November 13, 2026, the maintainer selected email OTP as the sole account-access
method, replacing the earlier email/password plus email OTP decision from #41.
Users of a gym app are expected to sign in infrequently and keep a renewable
session on their device, so avoiding a rarely used password is more useful than
offering multiple credential methods.

## Considered options

Email/password introduces password management and recovery for infrequent
sign-ins. Magic links require callback handling rather than code entry in the
app. Google and Apple OAuth introduce provider configuration and maintenance.
Email OTP serves both new and returning users without these additional flows.

## Account-access behavior

- One “Continue with email” flow serves new and returning users. Successful
  verification establishes access to a new account or signs into the existing
  account for that email; there is no separate registration form.
- Email codes contain six digits, expire after ten minutes, and can be requested
  again after a sixty-second cooldown shown in the UI. Wrong or expired codes
  leave the user able to retry or request another code.
- “Change email” returns to the populated email field, clears the entered code,
  and abandons the current attempt. Late responses from that attempt cannot
  advance the UI; another code request is required before verification in the
  new attempt. The earlier code remains valid at Supabase until it expires.
  The maintainer accepted this behavior instead of server-side cancellation.
- Conflicting actions are disabled while a request is pending. Unfinished
  sign-in attempts are not persisted across app restarts.
- Collect the account name after verification and before entering Templates
  when an account has no name. Allow editing the account name from Account.
  The signed-in Account screen shows account name, email, and Settings.
- Appearance Settings is also accessible before signing in.
- The [application User contract](../design.md#m1-database-scope-and-account-data-102)
  governs account-name storage and recovery if loading that User fails after
  successful verification. Auth metadata is not the authoritative name source.
- Password registration, password recovery, magic links, and OAuth are outside
  this account-access scope. In-app code verification needs no email callback.

## Navigation and session boundary

#42 introduces a signed-out account-access gate and opens Templates after
successful authentication and any required name collection. This supersedes
unrestricted sample browsing from the initial UI foundation.

“Indefinitely” means no application-imposed session lifetime or inactivity
timeout, using renewable sessions rather than non-expiring access tokens.
Sign-out, revoked credentials, or loss of the stored session require another
sign-in. [#43](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues/43) retains restoration
across launches, expiration handling, sign-out, and account-specific state cleanup.
Training-data persistence and account isolation remain in their feature tasks.

## Testing decisions

Use the existing route-level seam with an injected authentication service and
controlled clock. Drive real screens and navigation to cover code requests,
validation, resend cooldown, failures and retries, abandoned attempts, account
name collection/editing, and the signed-out gate. Assert externally observable
behavior rather than hook internals or implementation structure.

Supplement these tests with real Supabase verification of code emails and
authentication behavior. Configure code templates and timing consistently for
the local backend and hosted development project.

## References

- [Supabase email OTP](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-email-passwordless)
- [Supabase email templates](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-email-templates)
- [Supabase session behavior](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/sessions)
