> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

**Goal**  
A user can set up OpenFit and manage workout templates at the gym without a connection, with a local storage foundation for workout logging, history, and personal exercise maximums.

**Context**  
Implementation: agent. This specification replaces the initial architecture proposal in this issue. The existing account and template behavior is recorded in #43 and #45. The SQLite cutover is the prerequisite for the revised M2 work in #47, #48, and #49.

## Problem Statement

A user who relies on one phone at the gym has to sign in by email and depends on network access to browse the exercise catalog or save templates. A weak connection can interrupt planning and make saving unreliable. The app needs to support the full on-device training workflow from the first launch, including the illustrations users rely on when choosing or performing exercises.

## Solution

Replace Supabase and email authentication with on-device SQLite. Collect a display name during first launch, explain that data lives on this device and backup is unavailable, and greet the user on Templates. Ship the attributed RepDB catalog and illustrations with the app. Preserve the current template workflow and verify it on a device in airplane mode before building the M2 workout logging, history, and personal exercise maximum features on SQLite.

## User Stories

1. As a new user, I want to set up the app in airplane mode, so that I can start at the gym without a connection.
2. As a new user, I want to enter only my display name, so that setup feels personal and takes little time.
3. As a new user, I want a short notice about device storage and backup, so that I understand my recovery options before I start recording workouts.
4. As a returning user, I want the app to open directly to Templates and greet me by name, so that I can get started quickly.
5. As a user, I want to edit my display name in Settings, so that I can correct it and keep my training data.
6. As a new user, I want an empty template list, so that my templates contain only the workouts I create.
7. As a user on a fresh install, I want to search and filter the exercise catalog offline, so that I can find a movement even when the gym has no signal.
8. As a user choosing an exercise, I want to see its name, muscles, equipment, instructions, and available illustrations offline, so that I can understand how to perform it.
9. As a user inspecting a movement with two illustrated poses, I want to see both offline, so that I can review the movement from start to finish.
10. As a user planning a workout, I want to add and reorder template exercises and set weight and repetition targets offline, so that I can build a reusable template at the gym.
11. As a user, I want Save and Cancel to behave as they do today, so that I can tell saved templates from temporary drafts.
12. As a user, I want a failed save to keep my draft and let me retry, so that I can recover without re-entering the template.
13. As a user, I want a successful save to store the whole workout template, so that I always reopen a complete record.
14. As a returning user, I want saved templates and their exercise details to survive an app restart or update, so that I can keep using my plans.
15. As a user, I want to reopen, edit, and delete saved templates offline, so that I can maintain my plans wherever I train.
16. As a user, I want saved exercise details to remain stable when the bundled catalog changes, so that my prior plans and history retain their meaning.
17. As a user training offline, I want to start a workout session from a saved template, so that I can follow my planned exercises and targets.
18. As a user logging a workout, I want to check the indicator to log actual reps and weight for a set, so that I know which sets count as recorded.
19. As a user logging consecutive sets, I want the app to stay responsive during local saves, so that I can keep training.
20. As a user whose set save fails, I want my entered values to remain visible with a retry action, so that I can recover the record.

---
name: to-tickets
description: Break a plan, spec, or the current conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, published to the configured tracker (edges as text in one file per ticket locally, or native blocking links on a real tracker).
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# To Tickets

Break a plan, spec, or conversation into a set of **tickets**: tracer-bullet vertical slices, each declaring the tickets that **block** it.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes a reference (a spec path, an issue number or URL) as an argument, fetch it and read its full body and comments.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Ticket titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

Look for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. "Make the change easy, then make the easy change."

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the work into **tracer bullet** tickets.

<vertical-slice-rules>

- Each slice cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests): vertical, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Each slice is sized to fit in a single fresh context window
- Any prefactoring should be done first

</vertical-slice-rules>

Give each ticket its **blocking edges**: the other tickets that must complete before it can start. A ticket with no blockers can start immediately.

**Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing.** A **wide refactor** is one mechanical change (rename a column, retype a shared symbol) whose **blast radius** fans across the whole codebase, so a single edit breaks thousands of call sites at once and no vertical slice can land green. Don't force it into a tracer bullet; sequence it as **expand–contract**. First expand: add the new form beside the old so nothing breaks. Then migrate the call sites over in batches sized by blast radius (per package, per directory), each batch its own ticket blocked by the expand, keeping CI green batch to batch because the old form still exists. Finally contract: delete the old form once no caller remains, in a ticket blocked by every migrate batch. When even the batches can't stay green alone, keep the sequence but let them share an integration branch that all block a final integrate-and-verify ticket; green is promised only there.

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each ticket, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Blocked by**: which other tickets (if any) must complete first
- **What it delivers**: the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the blocking edges correct: does each ticket only depend on tickets that genuinely gate it?
- Should any tickets be merged or split further?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Publish the tickets to the configured tracker

Publish the approved tickets. **How** depends on the tracker `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configured; the tickets are the same either way, only the shape of the blocking edges changes:

- **Local files** → write one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` in dependency order (blockers first). Each file's "Blocked by" lists the numbers/titles it depends on. Use the per-ticket file template below: one ticket per file, never a single combined file.
- **A real issue tracker (GitHub, Linear, …)** → publish one issue per ticket in dependency order (blockers first) so each ticket's blocking edges can reference real identifiers. Use the platform's native blocking / sub-issue relationship where it has one; otherwise set each ticket's "Blocked by" to the blocking issues. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label unless instructed otherwise; the tickets are agent-grabbable by construction.

Work the **frontier**: any ticket whose blockers are all done. For a purely linear chain that means top to bottom.

Do NOT close or modify any parent issue.

<local-ticket-template>

# <NN>: <Ticket title>

**What to build:** the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective, not a layer-by-layer implementation list.

**Blocked by:** the numbers/titles of the tickets that gate this one, or "None (can start immediately)".

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [ ] Acceptance criterion 1
- [ ] Acceptance criterion 2

</local-ticket-template>

<issue-template>

## Parent

A reference to the parent issue on the tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).

## What to build

The end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective, not layer-by-layer implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Criterion 1
- [ ] Criterion 2

## Blocked by

- A reference to each blocking ticket, or "None (can start immediately)".

</issue-template>

In either form, avoid specific file paths or code snippets: they go stale fast. Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.
# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs live in [LibreLift/libre-lift](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues).
Use the `gh` CLI with `--repo LibreLift/libre-lift` for issue operations. The local
origin still uses the former `LibreLift/expo_suite` name, which GitHub redirects.

Read [project management](../project-mgmt.md) before tracker changes. Use its
issue templates, milestone rules, assignment process, and definition of done.

## Issue operations

- Read: `gh issue view NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --comments`.
- List: `gh issue list --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --state open --json number,title,labels,assignees`.
- Create: `gh issue create --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --title TITLE --body-file FILE --label LABEL`.
- Comment: `gh issue comment NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --body-file FILE`.
- Labels: `gh issue edit NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --add-label LABEL --remove-label LABEL`.
- Close: `gh issue close NUMBER --repo LibreLift/libre-lift --reason REASON`;
  use `completed` for delivered work or `not planned` for declined/superseded work.

Write multiline bodies to a file and pass `--body-file`. Use the matching
`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` structure. During triage, every published issue or comment
must start with `> *This was generated by AI during triage.*`.

## Project board

The board is [LibreLift MVP, organization project 1](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1).
Issue labels and board fields are separate. Use the mapping in
[triage labels](./triage-labels.md) for readiness and execution roles.

Inspect current fields with `gh project field-list 1 --owner LibreLift --format json`
and items with `gh project item-list 1 --owner LibreLift --format json`. Resolve
current project, field, item, and option IDs before a board edit; use
`gh project item-edit` for field changes. Check view filters before treating an
item as absent. Reuse the existing Status and Task Size fields and their options.

Project reads require the `read:project` token scope; writes require `project`.
If CLI access is unavailable, the public board can be inspected read-only. Report
blocked board edits and leave them pending rather than claiming synchronization.

## Dependencies and claiming work

Use native GitHub sub-issues for epics and native issue dependencies for blockers.
If unavailable, record `Part of #NUMBER` and `Blocked by: #NUMBER` links in the
issue body. A blocked task is not Ready. Apply `planned work` only with maintainer
authorization; follow the repository's assignment process before claiming work.

When a skill says to publish a spec or fetch a ticket, create or read a GitHub
issue in this repository. Follow repository label mappings instead of creating
labels named after a skill or its internal roles.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.**
# Triage roles: existing labels and board status

The skills' canonical roles map to combinations of existing labels, project
Status, issue state, and the implementation brief. This adapter replaces the
skills' default one-label-per-role convention; it creates no new labels or fields.

## Categories

- `bug`: a failure in existing behavior.
- `enhancement`: an improvement or new behavior.
- `documentation` and `accessibility` describe relevant subject matter; they do
  not substitute for a bug/enhancement classification during triage.

The bug-report template currently defaults to `documentation, needs triage`.
For an app bug, apply `bug` and retain `documentation` only if the report also
concerns documentation.

## State roles

| Canonical role | Existing labels | Project Status / issue state | Brief field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `needs-triage` | `needs triage` | Backlog; open | Maintainer evaluation pending |
| `needs-info` | `question` | Backlog; open | Identify the missing reporter information |
| `ready-for-agent` | `planned work` | Ready; open; prerequisites satisfied | `Implementation: agent` |
| `ready-for-human` | `planned work` | Ready; open; prerequisites satisfied | `Implementation: human`, with the reason |
| `wontfix` | `non-goal` for a scope rejection | Closed as `not planned` | Record why the request is declined |

`planned work` alone means accepted scope, not readiness or permission to start.
Agent-ready and human-ready work share existing labels and Status; distinguish
them in the brief rather than inferring an executor from `help wanted` or an assignee.
If the brief does not name an executor, resolve that before treating it as either
ready role. Remove the previous triage-state label when moving to a different role.

Use the existing execution statuses after work begins: In progress, In review,
and Done. Done follows the repository's definition of done; it is not a synonym
for any closed issue. Keep rejected requests out of Done; archive their Backlog
board items when removal from active views is authorized.

## Waiting and closure distinctions

- The live `question` description requests information from the issue author;
  use it for `needs-info`.
- The live `awaiting response` description means the issue author is waiting for
  a maintainer reply. Preserve it for that direction of communication; it is not
  an alias for `needs-info`.
- A duplicate uses `duplicate` and links the original issue. An already-delivered
  request points to the implementation. Neither automatically becomes `non-goal`.
- Deferred work stays in Backlog with its disposition explained; deferral alone
  is not a rejection.
- Preserve unrelated labels such as `epic` and `good first issue`.

If labels, the implementation brief, and board Status conflict, report the conflict
and ask the maintainer to resolve it before advancing the issue. Existing label
descriptions and the board's field names were checked on November 9, 2026.
# Project Management

The [LibreLift MVP project board](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1)
tracks planned work, priorities, and progress. Use the Plan view to see task sizes
and milestone groupings, and the Backlog view to follow workflow states. Check
the view's filters if an expected issue is not visible.

## Requests and triage

Use the repository's issue templates to report a problem, suggest a feature, or
request a documentation change. Feature and bug templates apply `needs triage`;
a request is not a commitment to implement it.

Maintainers review requests for scope, clarity, duplicates, and dependencies.
They ask for missing context, explain decisions on the issue, and either close
the request with a reason, defer it, or turn accepted work into actionable tasks.
Only maintainers apply `planned work`, so contributors can distinguish agreed
work from requests still under discussion. When a broad request is replaced by
smaller tasks, link the replacements and explain that closing the request does
not mean its implementation is complete.

## Planned work, epics, and milestones

Use the Task template for agreed work. Each task should describe its goal,
context and related design links, checkable acceptance criteria, dependencies,
and where to start. Size tasks with the board's Task Size field: XS is up to
one hour, S is two hours, M is four hours, L is seven hours, and XL is more than
seven hours. Split work that contains independently useful, reviewable changes.

Group feature tasks under a parent issue labeled `epic`, using GitHub
sub-issues. Epics describe user-visible outcomes; shared setup tasks can remain
standalone when several epics depend on them. Link dependencies so contributors
can see what must be finished first.

Assign planned work to the milestone it supports:

- **M1: Runnable Demo — November 18, 2026:** account access, exercise selection,
  and creating, saving, reopening, editing, and deleting fixed-weight templates.
- **M2: MVP — December 2, 2026:** workout logging and history, personal exercise
  maximums, percentage-based targets, and deferred catalog caching/retry work.

The M1 milestone description records capacity, estimates, and scope cuts.
Maintainers keep milestone assignments and board priorities aligned with that
budget. See the [roadmap](./roadmap.md) for work beyond the MVP.

## Workflow states

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Backlog | Work is recorded but is not ready to start. |
| Ready | Scope and acceptance criteria are clear and prerequisites are available. |
| In progress | An assigned contributor is actively working on the issue. |
| In review | The implementation PR is ready for independent review. |
| Done | The change has met the [definition of done](./git-standards.md#definition-of-done). |

Keep issue and board status current as work moves. A blocked task should not be
treated as ready until its prerequisites are resolved. Closed requests that were
superseded or declined should be distinguished from completed implementation in
their closing explanation.

## Labels and choosing work

| Label | How to use it |
| --- | --- |
| `needs triage` | A request awaits a maintainer's decision. |
| `planned work` | Maintainer-approved work available for planning and assignment. |
| `epic` | A parent issue grouping work by the value it delivers. |
| `good first issue` | A task intended to help newcomers get started; check dependencies and Ready status before choosing it. |
| `enhancement` | A feature suggestion or improvement; check triage status before implementing it. |
| `documentation` | A documentation addition or correction. |
| `help wanted` | Community assistance is requested. |
| `question` | Further information is requested from the issue author. |
| `awaiting response` | The issue author is waiting for communication from a maintainer. |

Start with an unassigned Ready task, preferably a `good first issue` for your
first contribution. Read its acceptance criteria and dependencies, then request
assignment through GitHub Discussions as described in the
[communication standards](./communication-standards.md). Ask about blocked
work before starting it to avoid duplicating effort.

{"body":"> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

**Goal**  
A user can set up OpenFit and manage workout templates at the gym without a connection, with a local storage foundation for workout logging, history, and personal exercise maximums.

**Context**  
Implementation: agent. This specification replaces the initial architecture proposal in this issue. The existing account and template behavior is recorded in #43 and #45. The SQLite cutover is the prerequisite for the revised M2 work in #47, #48, and #49.

## Problem Statement

A user who relies on one phone at the gym has to sign in by email and depends on network access to browse the exercise catalog or save templates. A weak connection can interrupt planning and make saving unreliable. The app needs to support the full on-device training workflow from the first launch, including the illustrations users rely on when choosing or performing exercises.

## Solution

Replace Supabase and email authentication with on-device SQLite. Collect a display name during first launch, explain that data lives on this device and backup is unavailable, and greet the user on Templates. Ship the attributed RepDB catalog and illustrations with the app. Preserve the current template workflow and verify it on a device in airplane mode before building the M2 workout logging, history, and personal exercise maximum features on SQLite.

## User Stories

1. As a new user, I want to set up the app in airplane mode, so that I can start at the gym without a connection.
2. As a new user, I want to enter only my display name, so that setup feels personal and takes little time.
3. As a new user, I want a short notice about device storage and backup, so that I understand my recovery options before I start recording workouts.
4. As a returning user, I want the app to open directly to Templates and greet me by name, so that I can get started quickly.
5. As a user, I want to edit my display name in Settings, so that I can correct it and keep my training data.
6. As a new user, I want an empty template list, so that my templates contain only the workouts I create.
7. As a user on a fresh install, I want to search and filter the exercise catalog offline, so that I can find a movement even when the gym has no signal.
8. As a user choosing an exercise, I want to see its name, muscles, equipment, instructions, and available illustrations offline, so that I can understand how to perform it.
9. As a user inspecting a movement with two illustrated poses, I want to see both offline, so that I can review the movement from start to finish.
10. As a user planning a workout, I want to add and reorder template exercises and set weight and repetition targets offline, so that I can build a reusable template at the gym.
11. As a user, I want Save and Cancel to behave as they do today, so that I can tell saved templates from temporary drafts.
12. As a user, I want a failed save to keep my draft and let me retry, so that I can recover without re-entering the template.
13. As a user, I want a successful save to store the whole workout template, so that I always reopen a complete record.
14. As a returning user, I want saved templates and their exercise details to survive an app restart or update, so that I can keep using my plans.
15. As a user, I want to reopen, edit, and delete saved templates offline, so that I can maintain my plans wherever I train.
16. As a user, I want saved exercise details to remain stable when the bundled catalog changes, so that my prior plans and history retain their meaning.
17. As a user training offline, I want to start a workout session from a saved template, so that I can follow my planned exercises and targets.
18. As a user logging a workout, I want to check the indicator to log actual reps and weight for a set, so that I know which sets count as recorded.
19. As a user logging consecutive sets, I want the app to stay responsive during local saves, so that I can keep training.
20. As a user whose set save fails, I want my entered values to remain visible with a retry action, so that I can recover the record.
21. As a user who backgrounds the app during a workout, I want to return straight to it, so that locking my phone does not interrupt the flow.
22. As a user who relaunches after app closure or an update, I want a prominent Resume workout action, so that I can recover my active workout session.
23. As a user returning to an interrupted workout, I want my saved checked sets restored, so that I can pick up where I left off.
24. As a user with an active workout session, I want to resume or stop it before starting another, so that I can keep my records clear.
25. As a user reviewing a session, I want its elapsed duration to run from start to finish or stop, so that time away from the app is included.
26. As a user, I want finished and stopped workout sessions to appear in history, so that I can review what I recorded offline.
27. As a user, I want editing or deleting a template to leave previous workout sessions intact, so that history reflects the workout I performed.
28. As a user, I want personal exercise maximums and percentage-based targets to survive restarts, so that I can continue using the same reference weights.

## Implementation Decisions

- Replace the app's Supabase runtime, authenticated HTTP persistence, and account-scoped state with a single local database using `expo-sqlite` and versioned schema migrations. Remove email entry and codes, authentication restoration, and sign-out. Keep the injected asynchronous service boundary used by screens and ViewModels.
- On first launch, collect a required, nonblank display name. On the name screen, show a small pop-up explaining that training data is stored on this device and backup is unavailable. Save the name locally, open Templates, and greet the user there. Subsequent launches open Templates directly. Settings allows changing the display name without changing training data.
- Bundle a pinned version of the free-tier RepDB catalog and all flat illustrations from the official package, including both poses where available. Keep visible attribution. First-launch search, filters, instructions, and illustrations use packaged assets. Preserve the namespaced catalog identity and independent placement identities and snapshots.
- Preserve user-visible template behavior from #45, including empty initial data, ordered placements and sets, fixed targets, saved exercise details, temporary drafts, and useful retry behavior. Save each complete template atomically and preserve its identity across edits. Keep drafts available after a failed save.
- After template parity is verified, use the same local persistence foundation for #47 and #49. #48 builds the workout flow. A workout session contains independent copies of its planned targets and exercise details. Completed or stopped sessions form workout history. Personal exercise maximums are keyed by catalog identity, and a percentage-based template target retains its percentage.
- Allow one active workout session. Checking the set indicator records the entered weight and repetitions. Use an asynchronous local write for the set. Restore only successfully saved checked sets after interruption. Keep values visible and offer retry after a failed write. Require the user to resume or stop the current session before starting another.
- Returning from the background takes the user straight back to the active workout. After app closure or an update that relaunches the app, Templates shows a prominent **Resume workout** action. Calculate duration from the start timestamp through finish or stop, including time away.
- The Supabase project holds disposable personal test data. The local cutover begins with empty training data and requires no migration or dual-write period.

## Testing Decisions

- Use the existing Expo Router integration seam. Drive real screens with injected services to verify the onboarding notice, display-name validation and editing, Templates greeting, catalog selection, template CRUD, and preservation of drafts on failure. Follow the existing onboarding, catalog search/detail, and persisted-template route tests. Assert user-visible outcomes.
- Use the agreed native acceptance gate with an installed app on a supported physical device in airplane mode. From a fresh launch, enter a name, use the catalog including both poses where offered, create and save a template, force-close the app, then reopen, edit, and delete the template using the real SQLite service. Verify saved data across an app update. Record the native build size impact of the bundled assets.
- In #47–#49, extend the same route and device seams for logged-set recovery, direct return from the background, the cold-launch Resume action, elapsed duration, stopped and completed session history, and personal exercise maximums and percentage targets. On device, check that rapid set logging remains responsive and that successfully saved checked sets reappear after a force-close.
- Run the checked-in TypeScript and Jest checks and the iOS and Android bundle checks during implementation. Native review exercises the installed app and real storage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Name onboarding, the local-storage notice, the Templates greeting, and editing the display name work without internet or email authentication.
- [ ] A fresh offline install can search and filter RepDB, read instructions, and display bundled flat illustrations, including both poses where available.
- [ ] The current template workflow passes on real SQLite in airplane mode. Saved templates survive restarts and updates, and failed saves preserve drafts for retry.
- [ ] The production app can launch and use templates without Supabase configuration.
- [ ] The M2 storage and workout follow-ups have clear SQLite requirements and follow the verified template cutover.

## Out of Scope

- Migrating existing Supabase data, carrying over existing accounts, or keeping an optional sign-in mode.
- Backup, export, restore, cross-device viewing, and synchronization in the MVP.
- Implementing the full M2 workout logging, history, exercise maximums, or percentage-target features in this cutover issue. Their product requirements above guide #47–#49.
- Redesigning the template editor or hosting a separate exercise dataset service.

## Further Notes

ADR 0006 records the architecture decision. The existing decisions about injected services, independent workout history, and saved exercise snapshots still apply. Split implementation into reviewable increments under the repository's contribution rules.

roadmap follows the project proposal's feature priorities: P0 is the minimum viable
product (MVP), P1 is the next step, and P2 is longer-term exploration. Work after
the MVP has no committed release dates.

## MVP

The semester MVP lets a user create and reuse workout templates using exercises
from a catalog, start workout sessions using existing templates, and review saved
workout history. It also supports recording exercise maximums and calculating
target weights as percentages of those maximums. These functions are available
without a subscription or payment.

| [M2: MVP](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/milestone/2) | December 2, 2026 | Start a workout from a saved template, record actual weights and repetitions, complete or stop the workout, and review its saved history. Record personal exercise maximums and use percentages to calculate template target weights. |

Templates and workout history must persist across app restarts. Editing or reusing
a template must not alter previously logged workouts. The first milestone covers
the complete template-creation workflow; the second adds the workout-logging
workflow and percentage-based planning.

on these core workflows within the available development time. Contributors can
help with implementation, testing, and documentation; see the
[contribution guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) and
[project board](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1) for how to get involved
and what work is currently planned.

are established. Their order below follows the CP3 proposal.

I’d split [#136](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/136) into **six tickets, one PR each**. The app switches to SQLite once the full template workflow is ready. The earlier PRs can be verified through the existing screens with the local service injected.

1. **Bundle the offline exercise catalog** · **Blocked by:** None. Replace the live fetch with pinned RepDB data and attributed flat illustrations. Verify search, filters, instructions, and both poses where available in an installed app in airplane mode. Record the build size impact.
2. **Create and reopen workout templates in SQLite** · **Blocked by:** None. Use the existing editor to save a complete template locally and reopen it after restarting. Verify atomic saves, stable identities, ordered sets, and saved exercise details.
3. **Edit and delete SQLite workout templates** · **Blocked by:** 2. Complete template parity through the existing editor, including reordering exercises, preserving drafts when a save fails, and retrying without duplicate or partial records.
4. **Switch the app to local onboarding and storage** · **Blocked by:** 1 and 3. Replace sign-in with required display-name entry and the backup notice, greet the user on Templates, and support name edits in Settings. Switch the default app to SQLite and verify the full template workflow after a force-close and an app update, in airplane mode. **This is the M2 gate.**
5. **Remove the retired Supabase app integration** · **Blocked by:** 4. Remove unused auth and client code, dependencies, and obsolete app-side tests. Verify the app builds and runs without Supabase configuration.
6. **Retire the repository’s Supabase tooling** · **Blocked by:** 4. Remove obsolete backend tooling and update contributor setup and verification instructions for SQLite. Hosted project deletion is a separate maintainer action.

I’d keep [#47](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/47), [#48](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/48), and [#49](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/49) as the existing M2 follow-ups. You have been provided a spec. This spec should have tickets associated with it, describing how to implement the spec.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

The goal is the entire spec implemented on a single **integration branch**, with every ticket resolved the way the issue tracker closes work.

The tickets are not a list of steps. They are a **task graph** with blocking relationships between them. This means there is always a **frontier** of tickets which are ready to be grabbed.

Communication to and from subagents should be sparse. Communicate primarily through **context pointers**: to the spec, tickets, research notes, and previous commits. Don't duplicate information already available via pointers.

**Implementer subagents** should be run in the background where possible for maximum concurrency.

## Steps

1. Read the spec and tickets to understand the task graph.

2. (optional) Use an **exploration subagent** to conduct any exploration required by the tickets - relevant codebase files or external documentation. Ensure the exploration subagent can save files - it should save its markdown notes in a directory outside the repo, accessible by all future subagents. This lets **implementer subagents** focus on implementation rather than exploration.

3. Create the integration branch. If the issue tracker closes work through PRs, or the user asks for one, open a draft PR after the first merge in step 5 (a branch with no commits ahead of main can't open one), marked as closing the spec and tickets.

4. Use **implementer subagents** to implement each ticket, each in its own worktree on its own branch. Each implementer subagent:
   - confirms its worktree is based on the integration branch before starting, and resets onto it if not;
   - calls the Skill tool with `tdd` to build the ticket;
   - merges the integration branch tip into its own branch before reporting done

5. Once an **implementer subagent** completes, merge its work to the integration branch with a **merger subagent**.

6. If this changes the **frontier** of available tickets, kick off more **implementer subagents** to work on the new tickets. This allows for maximum concurrency.

7. Once all tickets are complete, call the Skill tool with `code-review` on the integration branch. Fix all issues raised by the code review in a single **implementer subagent**.

8. If a draft PR exists, mark it ready for review. Otherwise, resolve each ticket the way the issue tracker closes work, and report the integration branch.

9. Clean up all **implementer subagent** worktrees.

description: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
---

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `GLOSSARY.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams: where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

```markdown

```

## Sections

Skip all preambles and keep prose brief. Use the user's domain language from `GLOSSARY.md`.

### Summary

Pick the smallest view that makes the key point clear.

- Show logic or an algorithm as pseudocode:

```text
on(save)
  if content is unchanged
    return cached result
  write new content
  return fresh result
```

- Show runtime control flow as a call tree:

```text
submitForm
  createSession
    persistPrompt
    launchAgent
  navigateToSession
```

- Show UI structure as a component tree, including state and module boundaries that matter:

```text
<SessionPage> (apps/example/src/routes/session.tsx)
  useSessionEvents()
  <SessionToolbar>
    <RunSkillButton> (packages/ui)
```

- Show file responsibility or a broad refactor as a shallow file tree:

```text
src/
├── commands/       # parses user actions
├── sessions/       # owns session state
└── transport/      # sends API requests
```

- Show component interaction, control flow, or data flow with Mermaid:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant UI
    participant Daemon
    User->>UI: choose command
    UI->>Daemon: send expanded prompt
    Daemon-->>UI: stream result
```

- Use `diff` when the point is what changes and the surrounding shape already exists. Match the diff shape to the topic.

For a component change:

```diff
 <SessionPage>
   useSessionEvents()
   <SessionToolbar>
+    <RunSkillButton />
   <SessionTimeline>
+    <SkillResultCard />
```

For a file-layout change:

```diff
 src/
 ├── commands/
+│   └── show-me.ts       # expands the slash command
 ├── sessions/
-└── transport.ts
+└── transport/
+    ├── client.ts
+    └── stream.ts
```

For a call-tree or call-stack change:

```diff
 submitForm
   createSession
     persistPrompt
+    expandSkillMention
     launchAgent
-  navigateToSession
+  navigateToSession
+    subscribeToEvents
```

For a state or control-flow change:

```diff
 on(save)
-  write content
+  if content is unchanged
+    return cached result
+  write new content
+  invalidate cache
```

- Show the whole block when most of it is new, when omitted context would hide ownership or order, or when the user needs a copyable target shape:

```ts
function expandSkill(command: string): string {
  const skillName = command.slice(1);
  return `use the ${skillName} skill`;
}
```

#### Guidance

Place each visual next to the short text it supports. Keep only the calls, files, props, states, and boundaries needed to answer the user's current question or the options to resolve the current discussion point.

You may use one of these, you may use several, it is unlikely you will use all of them. Use your judgement and don't overwhelm the user.

### Evidence

Concrete evidence that the change works. Show a before and after.

Screenshots are S-tier - when the environment is set up for it and the change is visual.

Execution-based evidence is A-tier. Test results, console output. Show the exact test that now fails and passes, using pseudocode.

### Merge Danger

Describe whether it's a one-way or two-way door. You can walk back through two-way doors, but not one-way doors. A PR that is cheap to roll back is lower risk. Changes that involve destructive actions or hard-to-reverse decisions are one-way doors.

The blast radius is the potential impact or scope of the changes introduced by this PR. Consider all possibilities. Examples are layout shift, breakages for consumers, mobile responsiveness, etc.

name: code-review
description: "Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to \"review since X\"."
---

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards**: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec**: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.), fetched via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below: a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name**: a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code**: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy**: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps**: the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession**: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches**: the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery**: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change**: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality**: abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains**: long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man**: a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest**: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

**Standards sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full (the sub-agent has no other access to it).
- The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

Saved templates previously reset to demonstration data on app reload. Production now stores complete account-private templates through the existing editor, preserving exercise snapshots, placement identities, order, and fixed-weight targets across renewed access to the same backend.

```text
editor → account-scoped service → authenticated Edge Function
       → requesting-user data access → atomic database save + retry recognition
```

Unchanged retries recover the original committed result; edited drafts use a new operation against the same template. Concurrent distinct saves use last-committed whole-template replacement. # Offline exercise catalog verification

The catalog uses the schema v3 JSON in `@repdb/exercises@2026.11.1`. The
existing mapper accepted all 708 records without diagnostics. The package
contains 523 start/peak pairs and 185 single illustrations. The catalog screen
links to RepDB for attribution.

`npm ci` generates a Metro index with a static import reference for every
packaged flat WebP. On display, the gallery resolves matching RepDB image paths
to native assets. Snapshots retain the existing string references, names,
instructions, and targets. An earlier snapshot with the same RepDB path also
uses the bundled image. Other legacy URLs remain usable when reachable, and
their saved details remain readable if the image fails.

## Bundle evidence

iOS and Android passed `expo export` and the production-mode
`expo export:embed` step used by native builds. The embedded asset output for
each platform contained 1,231 WebP files whose SHA-256 hashes matched the
package. Together the images add 20,278,684 bytes (19.34 MiB) per platform before
packaging. The regular export stores 1,203 unique WebP payloads
(19,804,900 bytes) because 28 files share identical contents.

Compared with integration base `0e508fb`, the regular export's Hermes bytecode
increased by 3,144,897 bytes on iOS and 3,145,098 bytes on Android. These
measurements cover exported artifacts. The signed app download and installed
size were unmeasured.

## Device acceptance

Router tests exercise offline search, filtering, instructions, navigation,
both packaged poses, and saved template detail. No supported physical device
was connected, so native decoding and installed-app behavior in airplane mode
remain unverified. For this slice, enter the authenticated catalog before
going offline. From an installed build in airplane mode, search and filter,
open a single illustration and both poses of a paired exercise, read the
instructions, and return to the filtered list. The full fresh-install and saved
template airplane-mode check requires the local onboarding and SQLite cutover
in [#136](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/136).

[Verification record](/Users/james/.t3/worktrees/open-fit/t3-b5ce5b46-b513d41db8e03329/docs/issue-141-local-onboarding.md)

The cutover passed automated tests with the production SQLite wiring. The implementation uses an inline storage notice, so I’ll change it to the small pop-up we agreed on before publishing the slice. Physical-device verification is still pending.

# Vercel React Best Practices

Comprehensive performance optimization guide for React and Next.js applications, maintained by Vercel. Contains 70 rules across 8 categories, prioritized by impact to guide automated refactoring and code generation.

## When to Apply

Reference these guidelines when:
- Writing new React components or Next.js pages
- Implementing data fetching (client or server-side)
- Reviewing code for performance issues
- Refactoring existing React/Next.js code
- Optimizing bundle size or load times

## Rule Categories by Priority

| Priority | Category | Impact | Prefix |
|----------|----------|--------|--------|
| 1 | Eliminating Waterfalls | CRITICAL | `async-` |
| 2 | Bundle Size Optimization | CRITICAL | `bundle-` |
| 3 | Server-Side Performance | HIGH | `server-` |
| 4 | Client-Side Data Fetching | MEDIUM-HIGH | `client-` |
| 5 | Re-render Optimization | MEDIUM | `rerender-` |
| 6 | Rendering Performance | MEDIUM | `rendering-` |
| 7 | JavaScript Performance | LOW-MEDIUM | `js-` |
| 8 | Advanced Patterns | LOW | `advanced-` |

## Quick Reference

### 1. Eliminating Waterfalls (CRITICAL)

- `async-cheap-condition-before-await` - Check cheap sync conditions before awaiting flags or remote values
- `async-defer-await` - Move await into branches where actually used
- `async-parallel` - Use Promise.all() for independent operations
- `async-dependencies` - Use better-all for partial dependencies
- `async-api-routes` - Start promises early, await late in API routes
- `async-suspense-boundaries` - Use Suspense to stream content

### 2. Bundle Size Optimization (CRITICAL)

- `bundle-barrel-imports` - Import directly, avoid barrel files
- `bundle-analyzable-paths` - Prefer statically analyzable import and file-system paths to avoid broad bundles and traces
- `bundle-dynamic-imports` - Use next/dynamic for heavy components
- `bundle-defer-third-party` - Load analytics/logging after hydration
- `bundle-conditional` - Load modules only when feature is activated
- `bundle-preload` - Preload on hover/focus for perceived speed

### 3. Server-Side Performance (HIGH)

- `server-auth-actions` - Authenticate server actions like API routes
- `server-cache-react` - Use React.cache() for per-request deduplication
- `server-cache-lru` - Use LRU cache for cross-request caching
- `server-dedup-props` - Avoid duplicate serialization in RSC props
- `server-hoist-static-io` - Hoist static I/O (fonts, logos) to module level
- `server-no-shared-module-state` - Avoid module-level mutable request state in RSC/SSR

    def git(*args, data=None):
        return subprocess.check_output(['git', *args], env=env, input=data).decode().strip()

    snapshots = []
    parent = base
    for ref, message, paths in layers:
        git('read-tree', head if paths is None else parent)
        if paths:
            patch = subprocess.check_output(['git', 'diff', '--binary', base, head, '--', *paths])
            git('apply', '--cached', '--binary', data=patch)
        tree = git('write-tree')
        commit = git('commit-tree', tree, '-p', parent, '-m', message)
        assert sum(int(value) for line in git('diff', '--numstat', parent, commit).splitlines()
                   for value in line.split('\t', 2)[:2]) <= 1000
        git('diff', '--check', parent, commit)
        snapshots.append((ref, commit, git('diff', '--shortstat', parent, commit)))
        parent = commit
    assert git('rev-parse', parent + '^{tree}') == git('rev-parse', head + '^{tree}')
    for ref, commit, stat in snapshots:
        git('update-ref', 'refs/heads/' + ref, commit)

# Local onboarding and SQLite verification

[#141](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/issues/141) switches the
production app to local display-name onboarding and uses SQLite for workout
templates. The app ships the RepDB catalog and flat illustrations. Workout
history still shows labeled samples.

## Verified in the worktree

- On Node 24.12.0, `npm ci`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (109 tests in 22
  suites), and `npx expo-doctor` (20 checks) passed.
- The Expo Router tests start the default app with a fresh database and use
  Node's SQLite engine with the Expo SQLite bridge substituted. With JavaScript
  fetch disabled, the tests dismiss the device storage and backup pop-up, require
  a nonblank display name, greet the user on Templates, inspect both poses of a
  bundled exercise, and save a template. They close the database, remount the
  app, reopen the template, edit it, and delete it.
- A pre-cutover SQLite schema version 2 fixture retains its saved template and
  set targets after migration. A name edited in Settings and the Dark
  appearance both survive an app remount. The remaining SQLite and router
  tests cover draft navigation, cancellation, reordering, snapshots, rollback,
  save retries, and sample history.
- Both iOS and Android Expo exports passed with the Supabase environment
  variables unset, dotenv loading disabled, and Expo offline mode enabled.
  Each bundle contains the local SQLite composition and RepDB instructions.
  Both export manifests reference all 1,203 RepDB illustrations, totaling
  19,804,900 bytes before application packaging. The Hermes bundles measure
  5,327,488 bytes for iOS and 5,317,600 for Android. Source maps contain no
  Supabase runtime or legacy account routes.
- Android release assembly passed from a clean copy of cutover revision
  `644b22d` using Expo prebuild and Gradle. The resulting universal APK was
  127,559,668 bytes. All 1,231 packaged RepDB illustrations matched their source
  WebP files by SHA-256. The APK was inspected locally without installing it.

At the time of this verification, the retired account implementation was
still present in the worktree.
`auth-navigation.test.tsx`, `auth-sessions.test.tsx`, and
`production-template-access.test.tsx` exercise the retired router and are
excluded from the active Jest and TypeScript checks for this run.

## Physical-device evidence pending

No iOS or Android device was available. Neither platform ran an installed build
during this verification. The native Expo SQLite bridge, first launch and
catalog rendering in airplane mode, force-close recovery, in-place app update,
and installed package size remain unverified. The database migration and
restart checks above ran through Jest. Follow the
[device-review steps](setup.md#device-review) to complete the offline
template-parity gate.

**Door** Two-way for the code. The cutover starts with an empty SQLite database. The previous hosted records are disposable test data and stay outside this PR.

## Description

OpenFit now opens with local display-name onboarding, uses SQLite for workout templates, and ships the attributed RepDB catalog and illustrations for offline use. Existing template screens keep their create, read, edit, delete, and retry behavior. Workout history remains labeled sample data until the M2 session work.

```text
Name onboarding → Templates → injected service → SQLite
                             ↘ bundled RepDB catalog and illustrations
```

## Related Issue Link

Closes #136. Closes #138. Closes #139. Closes #140. Closes #141. Closes #142. Closes #143.

- #145 reviews the offline exercise catalog (#138).
- #146 reviews SQLite template creation and reads (#139).
- #147 reviews SQLite template editing and deletion (#140).
- #148 reviews the production SQLite and name onboarding cutover (#141).
- #149 reviews retirement of the Supabase contributor workflow (#143).
- #150, #151, and #152 review Supabase app cleanup (#142) in three slices under 1,000 lines each.

The M2 briefs in #47, #48, and #49 now describe the SQLite and resume behavior. #141 remains the physical-device template-parity gate.

## PR Checklist

- [x] Changes are available as individual review slices
- [x] Integrated TypeScript and offline iOS and Android exports pass
- [x] All 99 Jest tests and 20 Expo Doctor checks pass
- [x] Setup and architecture documentation reflect the cutover
- [ ] Physical-device offline template-parity audit
- [ ] Review from one non-author contributor

## Additional Details

### Evidence

- The default router flow runs with JavaScript fetch disabled and uses real SQLite files via Node. It covers name entry, bundled illustrations, template CRUD, save retries, reopening, and schema upgrades. The native Expo SQLite bridge still requires the installed-app audit.
- The final integration rejects foreign and invented saved placement IDs and retains an unchanged committed retry after a newer edit removes a placement.
- Both final Expo exports passed with Supabase environment variables unset. Android release assembly passed for the cutover revision, and all 1,231 packaged RepDB illustrations matched the source files by SHA-256.
- No physical iOS or Android device was connected. The [device review](https://github.com/open-source-fitness/open-fit/blob/feat/136-local-storage/docs/setup.md#device-review) documents the remaining airplane-mode, force-close, and installed-update scenarios.

### Merge Danger

**Door** Two-way for the code. The cutover starts with an empty SQLite database. The previous hosted records are disposable test data and stay outside this PR.

**Blast radius** App startup, template persistence, and exercise catalog delivery.
